speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am rising today to implore the federal government to implement at least one of the recommendations of Canada's Auditor General. The government should immediately start giving taxpayers a score card on how we are doing in working to eliminate the deficit. Telling Canadians what our financial position is just once a year in a budget is not good enough. People paying high income taxes, business taxes, sales taxes, user fees, payroll taxes and surtaxes deserve a monthly or at least quarterly accounting. The government has to give us some hope that there is light at the end of the tunnel, that the deficit will be reduced to zero in so many months.
The Auditor General is right on this one and the Minister of Finance would do well to listen and then to take action.

Mr. Speaker, unemployment keeps rising in Quebec. In the riding of Chambly, Aliments Terra has closed its doors, resulting in 200 lay-offs. On January 3, Angus will close down in east Montreal, which means another 3,000 jobs lost. Joint action by governments is urgently needed to breathe new life into the economy of Montreal.
Last week's announcement, a pitiful $32 million per year for five years, is nowhere near being the kind of serious joint program we need to help the economy in Quebec.
The government must realize it has a duty to get involved in the recovery of Quebec's economy. I would ask all members of this House to do their homework before they get involved in this kind of discussion so they can make a constructive contribution to the debate. This is not patronage. It is a matter of elementary justice and common sense.

Mr. Speaker, I want to speak today about Canada's most important industry, northwestern Ontario's most important industry and Thunder Bay's most important industry.
Forestry is this country's single largest industry. It generates over $40 billion a year in sales. It accounts for about $20 billion yearly in export sales, all in U.S. funds. More than 800,000 Canadians are employed directly by this industry and 8,000 large and small businesses are directly involved in the forestry industry.
This industry is in serious difficulty today and government intervention is needed badly. What we need is a de-inking and recycling of facilities throughout this country. The future of Canada's industry and northwestern Ontario depends on being able to supply recycled products to all of our customers.
This government must act now before Canada's major industry is all but shut down.

Recently the Sisters of the Assumption celebrated 100 years of dedicated service to the people of the Four Nations of Hobbema in my constituency and also in western Canada.

I quote in part from a poem of thanks by Linda Cutknife:
- these Sisters have watched the community of Hobbema grow From rags to riches
They have shared our happiness and our pain.
They were with us when we buried our people in tragic times,
They offered us prayer and goodness
when we thought the world had gone insane. . .
We will never forget these Sisters
Who were sometimes our mothers, our friends, our teachers or whatever we wanted them to be.
They taught us how to pray to God,
How to talk to Jesus as a friend,
And they told us the story of how Jesus died so that we could be free-
In the spirit of national unity, I ask this House to join me and all my constituents in thanking the Sisters of the Assumption for all they have done to build a great nation.

Mr. Speaker, I am appalled to hear reports that the federal Department of Transport is considering the withdrawal of air traffic controllers from Charlottetown and 12 other airports across the county.
The reports suggest that the controllers may be withdrawn as early as February of next year.
Some 30,000 flights a year use the Charlottetown airport, and those people are entitled to the same level of service as enjoyed in the rest of the country.
The continual erosion of services in the outlying areas of this country shows us that this government is trying to fight its deficit problems on the backs of the poorest people and in the poorest regions of the country.
I call on the Minister of Transport to reject this recommendation and to assure Canadians in smaller centres that the level of service will remain the same for them as for other Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of importance to a number of constituents in the Cambridge area.
The Canadian horse is a national breed and is now endangered. There are approximately 1,100 in existence and of these 700 are 100 per cent pure. The Canadian horse is part of our heritage and was proclaimed the national breed by Parliament on March 17, 1909.
To promote the Canadian breed, to commemorate its place in our history and to remind Canadians of our natural heritage, the constituents of Cambridge would like to see a stamp series produced to honour the breed of horse known as the Canadian.
I ask that serious consideration be given to having the Canadian horse breed honoured by a stamp.

Mr. Speaker, "The Situation in Croatia", a report prepared by 11 of the 12 monitoring delegations, has overwhelmingly substantiated the charges that have been levelled against the Yugoslav army: targeting the sick, killing children, bulldozing villages.
Innocent civilians are clearly being confronted by an army run amok. How much longer is the international community going to stand aside? Where is the new world order that was supposed to be dawning but a short time ago?
The question is: Are we doomed forever to replay history? The answer must be no. The United Nations must take action. There must be a military interposition between the Yugoslav army and those who are being brutalized.
There must be a massive transfer of humanitarian assistance. The international community must rise to the challenge before it and Canada, if we are to be true to ourselves, must take the lead.
December 4, 1991	COMMONS

Mr. Speaker, yesterday the Canadian Parliamentary Friendship Group for Syrian Jewry was formed. Our group has Conservative, Liberal and New Democrat representatives who are deeply concerned about the plight of Jews in Syria.
Today I want to bring this grave situation to the attention of my colleagues in the House and all Canadians.
There are 4,500 Jews in Syria who are being denied the right to leave oppressive Syrian rule.

Jews living in Syria have been deprived of their basic rights. They cannot emigrate. They cannot travel freely and they cannot vote. They are jailed and tortured. Their correspondence and telephone conversations are censored, and their activities are watched very closely.

We must work together to ensure for all Syrian Jews that fundamental human rights are guaranteed, including their safe departure from Syrian oppression to freedom.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, fish plants in Glace Bay and Louisbourg are vital to our local economy.
The federal government should explain why it decided to increase cod quotas around Cape Breton Island for the French metropolitan fleet from St. Malo, France, in the past year and to cut cod quotas for Canadians.
The federal government should also withdraw a commitment given to France that it can catch 60 per cent of its entire year's cod quota around Cape Breton Island in the first three months of 1992.
Not only have the cod quotas been increased for France around Cape Breton Island, but foreign nations like Bulgaria and Poland have been given so-called

experimental licences to catch mackerel, with 30 per cent by-catch of capelin in the Sydney Bight in the past year.
The federal government has systematically destroyed the cod fishery around Cape Breton Island and in the gulf by issuing licences to Cuba to catch squid along the Nova Scotia coast and the U.S.S.R. to catch capelin. Both species are the food supply of the gulf cod stock.
Not one tonne of fish should be taken from Canadian quotas while Canada gives one ounce of quota to foreign nations around our coast.

Mr. Bill Attewell (Markham-Whitchurch-StoufF-
ville): Mr. Speaker, in a special report signed by 11 out of 12 European community members monitoring delegations, the Yugoslavian army is accused of deliberately targeting civilians, hospitals and schools in Croatia.
The report states these acts are brutal and have proven effective in terrorizing the people of Croatia. The report of last week entitled "The Situation in Croatia" condemns the Serb dominated Yugoslav force as a "cowardly army fighting no recognizable principle, but largely, instinctively for its own status and survival".
The report recommends that the 12-nation European community intervene militarily and punish the Yugoslav federal army. I believe we should go one step further. We must announce to these self-serving Communist officers of the Yugoslav army that a war tribunal will be set up to try the officers of either army who have committed war crimes.
The barbaric attacks and bloodshed against Croatians must end.

Mr. Speaker, last night I joined the Ukrainian Canadian community on the steps of Parliament in celebrating the independence of Ukraine. Today on those same steps over 2,000 Croatian Canadians were asking their government why Canada and the world continue to refuse to recognize the independence of Croatia after 94 per cent of the people of Croatia and Slovenia voted for freedom and nationhood earlier this year.

December 4, 1991
A European community report just released accuses the Yugoslav army of targeting civilians, hospitals, and schools in Croatia in an effort to terrorize the population.
While Croatia must of course fully respect the rights of the Serbian minority, it is those of the Croatian majority who are being brutally denied. Canada must urge the United Nations to immediately intervene to stop the bloodshed. Canada must provide desperately needed humanitarian aid directly to the people of Croatia, and Canada must end its silence and ensure that the will of the people of Croatia and Slovenia for freedom, democracy and independence is realized at last.

Mr. Speaker, on December 1 the world watched a remarkable event unfold in Ukraine: the decision by a freedom loving people through a democratic process to join the world community as an independent nation.
Our Prime Minister realized the importance of this moment immediately and recognized the birth of the new republic of Ukraine.
The London Ukrainian community joins the chorus of millions around the world congratulating the Prime Minister and Canada. Congratulations, Prime Minister, for again demonstrating the kind of leadership Canada is renowned for throughout the world.
Will the Prime Minister exercise his bold leadership once again and now recognize the republic of Croatia?

Mr. Speaker, last week the federal government announced it would give Quebec $160 million over a period of five years. This means $32 million per year, or $5 per person per year in Quebec. It is not enough, considering the damage done to Quebec's economy by federal policies.
Furthermore, the critical comments of the New Democrats and Liberals were biased and inappropriate. Did Quebecers criticize the fact that the government sent $800 million to Western Canada? No, Mr. Speaker. Quebec merely wants its fair share of the taxes it pays to Ottawa. It does not want handouts and it only wishes it could keep all its tax money and spend it according to its own priorities.

ORGANIZATION OF ECONOMIC CO-OPERATION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am happy to inform the House today of developments this week at a meeting of the Organization of Economic Co-operation and Development, the OECD, in Paris.
The Minister of State for the Environment, led the Canadian delegation, was vice-chair of the meeting. The theme of this important meeting of environment and development ministers of the 24 member countries of the OECD was a partnership for sustainable development.
On Monday the Minister urged her colleagues from the OECD countries to work to develop new global partnerships to achieve sustainable development.
Canada is well positioned to lead in partnerships with private sector organizations, business, industry, labour, educators and institutions.
The central position and prominence of the OECD as an institution and of its member countries will cast it in a number of key roles leading up to the United Nations Conference on Environment and Development and beyond. Canada will continue to be active and committed to these initiatives.

December 4, 1991

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a question for the Acting Prime Minister. Yesterday the Prime Minister met the premier of British Columbia who became the fifth provincial premier to call for a first ministers' conference on the economy. We also heard that Premier Bourassa of Quebec said he would be willing to attend such a conference, if it were likely to produce positive results.
As we see now that provincial premiers representing the three main political parties in Canada are ready right now to meet the Prime Minister to discuss economic problems, why does the government refuse to hold such a conference which might find a way to get out of this unending recession?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister will not refuse a meeting with the premiers. He already met with some premiers last week and other meetings are scheduled for the coming days. A meeting with the premiers to consider the economy is possible.

The Prime Minister said yesterday that he would be reflecting on the advice of the finance minister who will be meeting with the provincial finance ministers on December 11 and 12. He will be reflecting on the views that have been expressed to him by the premiers with whom he has been meeting.
The Minister of Finance said in the scrum yesterday: "If he thinks a meeting would be beneficial, I would be happy to call it".

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to ask a question of the minister again. Yesterday the Prime Minister made a speech in Vancouver and he said, among other things, that "Canadians are going to have to fish or cut bait" about the future of Canada.
Oral Questions
I agree entirely with the Prime Minister. But if the Prime Minister really believes, as I do, that all Canadians must have the chance to say yes to Quebec and to say yes to Canada, why has he pulled the plug on the proposal that I made in good faith to have a national referendum where all the people of Canada can vote on the future of this country?

Mr. Speaker, according to Canadian Press, the Prime Minister said in Vancouver yesterday that the Speech from the Throne promised consultation with Canadians. The Speech from the Throne does not say what form that consultation will take. We are still looking at the various options. We have not ruled any out. But we are honouring that promise made in the Speech from the Throne.

Perhaps the Leader of the Opposition missed the response yesterday by my colleague, the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs, to the member for Annapolis Valley-Hants, but he made it abundantly clear, as has the Prime Minister, that all options remain open.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I would like to put a question to the minister who is replacing the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs. Would the government not be prepared right now to clarify the situation and to make people understand that what we want is a double majority referendum, where every region of Canada- the Atlantic, Quebec, Ontario and the west-could say yes to Quebec and yes to Canada at the same time? Why does the government not propose such a solution immediately since no one knows exactly what the government wants to do, which is creating confusion, and since it is high time to find a positive solution to save this country?

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. Leader of the Opposition points out, he and his party have locked themselves into the position that there must be a referendum on a particular formula. What the Prime Minister and the Minister responsible for Constitutional Affairs have indicated is that we favour the broadest possible constructive consultation with Canadians. I put the emphasis upon constructive, in that any action that we take must be one that helps to unite Canadians and not to divide them or to polarize them.

December 4, 1991
Oral Questions
It is incumbent on all of us on all sides of this House to do what we can to bring Canadians into the process, to solicit their participation and to do what we can to unite Canadians, not to put barriers between them.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The minister will know that Canada Post employees in London, Ontario are routinely asked to use someone else's name and social insurance number to do contract work for the post office after working hours.
Given that this action by Canada Post contravenes the Canada Labour Code, the collective agreement, the Income Tax Act and probably many other statutes of Canada, when did the minister find out about this practice and what has he done to stop it?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member should know that Revenue Canada, through its matching programs, will identify any such potential problems or inequities that exist. We found out about those in recent days. We are currently investigating the matter to the best of our ability.
Upon the conclusion of the investigation, appropriate action will be taken. Every step to protect the individual is being taken at this present time.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the culprit here is not the employees in question. They were counselled by Canada Post and Canada Post has admitted to this publicly.
I have in hand here a cheque which was given to Mr. Mike Bellemy and the cheque is made to his mother, Audrey Bellemy, a senior citizen.

I want to ask the minister opposite what action the government will take not to punish employees but to reassure Canadians that Canada Post obeys the law?

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto Jelinek (Minister of National Revenue):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all, if the hon. member or any other member has any additional evidence to give to us, we would be happy to receive it and include it in the ongoing investigation.
I repeat to the hon. member and to Canadians who are affected by this situation that a matching program after the fact does take place and appropriate action will be taken. In any event, if the hon. member has any additional information I would be very happy to look at it.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Acting Prime Minister.
The Leader of the Opposition continues to talk about a referendum on the Constitution and the Prime Minister speaks of public consultation. But the country's future is not just the Constitution. You need only listen to people. The real problems are finding work and the economy.
This government's economic record is a complete failure. When will this government hold the only national referendum that really counts; when will the government call an election?
Hear, hear.

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International TVade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in due course.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
The previous minister spoke about the broadest possible consultation. There is one form of broad consultation and every indication says that this government has failed in every part of this country and especially on the economy. When the government stood up in the past and said it was on the right track, we have to ask who it is speaking for: the banks that had a billion dollar profit or the $27 billion in corporate taxes that were not paid?
December 4, 1991

Who is the minister listening to because he is certainly not speaking for those Canadians who want full participation through an election? When will the government call an election for that full participation?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Trade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this type of political game does not amuse Canadians. What Canadians are looking for is consultation about the economy and that is precisely what we are engaged in with the prosperity initiative that is having meetings in communities.
I had a meeting in my hon. friend's community and I would say to her that it was a very successful meeting. People came out to that meeting, gave their views on how we should deal with international markets, how we should deal with training, how we should deal with technology and how we get investment to produce jobs in communities such as hers. It is that type of dialogue among Canadians that is going to generate the change of attitude that is necessary within the country.
I think we should move on.

Mr. Speaker, I have a supplementary question.
What Canadians want is action. Canadians are not getting action on the economy and they are not finding jobs. Today Statistics Canada reported that the number of jobs available has not changed from last month and in the last year the number of jobs available across this country has gone down from 12 per cent to 26 per cent. It means fewer jobs are available for Canadians.
The kind of action Canadians want is action on the economy and they want this government to do something. Every indication is that this government will not take-

I wonder if the hon. member would put her question, please.
Oral Questions
The government will take the action and so I say to the minister responsible: Will the government call an election and stand up and ask the people for their real opinion?

speakeroldname: Hon. Michael Wilson (Minister of Industry, Science and Technology and Minister for International Thade):
speakerposition: Minister for International Trade; Minister of Industry, Science and Technology
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the fact that interest rates have come down over 6 percentage points since May of last year indicates action on the part of the government.
My hon. friend talks about the need to create jobs. There have been 101,000 jobs created since February of this year. So jobs are being created.
My hon. friend talks about what is happening in the economy. Housing starts have been above 150,000 now for six or seven months. They reached 200,000 one month during the summer. So things are changing.
I think we are going to have to move on.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to raise two very compelling international matters with the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
First, the European community monitoring group has reported that violence against Croatians persists and that measures taken to stop the random terrorism of the Yugoslav army have failed.
I want to ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, on behalf of Canada: Will she call for an immediate emergency meeting of the security council to ensure the UN force will be sent right away to protect the lives of Croatian civilians?
Second, will she personally meet with foreign ministers of the European community to discuss the intention and the timing of their recognition of Croatia and Slovenia?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first of all it is very important that we all recognize the horror of what is going on in Croatia and in other parts of Yugoslavia.
I have been in touch with our ambassador at the United Nations. I was in touch with him this morning. There is a security council meeting to receive a report from Cyrus Vance on his return from Yugoslavia. He is expected to be in New York tomorrow. He is spending another day in the region in a further attempt to ensure that the cease-fire holds. He and his number two man are in Croatia, in Zagreb.

Oral Questions
I have also spoken to our own ambassador in Yugoslavia and instructed him to seek permission from the Croatian authorities to visit Croatia himself and report directly back to me. I should say that no foreign ambassador located in Belgrade has visited Croatia, partly at the request of the Croatian authorities. Therefore, I have made this a personal message from myself to the Croatian authorities via the ambassador and I want a report back from him directly.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps the minister should consider sending a special delegation to Croatia to examine the situation.
I also want to ask this question. On both sides of this House and throughout the country we all welcome the release of western hostages with one exception. A Canadian, Mrs. Henriette Haddad, is still being held hostage after six years of detention without much hope of being released.
I want to ask the minister why she personally has kept silent on this issue. Why has the Canadian government not had Mrs. Haddad put on the list of UN hostages that are being negotiated? Will she take action immediately, while there is still time, to have Mrs. Haddad become part of a deal involving western hostages who are to be freed this week?

speakeroldname: Hon. Barbara McDougall (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, we have discussed Mrs. Haddad with the United Nations. My chief of staff has met with Mrs. Haddad's family. I should say that Mrs. Haddad's son visited a member of Parliament in 1985 about his mother's disappearance and then again in 1987. He was not in touch with us again until this year, even though we had searched for Mrs. Haddad through all our known connections, including terrorist organizations.
No organization in Syria or in Lebanon or in any other part of the region has come forward and said that it is holding Mrs. Haddad despite our efforts to locate her and to discuss-
Put her on the list.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I sometimes wonder if the hon. member really does care about this.
We have followed this up with the United Nations. We have followed this up with all of our contacts through Syria and Lebanon and indeed through the groups that are known to hold hostages. There is absolutely no trace of Mrs. Haddad that we can find and we are continuing to pursue it.
 * *

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Associate Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development in the absence of the minister.
The Auditor General's report states that this government has never increased funding for aboriginal housing despite an increase in the aboriginal population three times the national average.
Will the ministers quit avoiding and neglecting their responsibilities and will they act by providing now the funding so desperately needed for aboriginal housing?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was asked a similar question yesterday by a member of the NDP, and it will of course be a pleasure to give the hon. member the requisite information. We realize that aboriginal communities have tremendous needs in terms of housing. Our investment in this area has already been very substantial, and yesterday I quoted some rather impressive figures which reflect this government's commitment to helping improve aboriginal housing. The government has spent between $120 and $140 million annually, and so far 3,000 new houses have been built. Funds have also been made available for the renovation of another 3,000 to 4,000 houses.
December 4, 1991

Oral Questions
That being said, we realize that we are scarcely meeting the demand. As the hon. member probably knows, we are involved in discussions. A report was produced by the department, and aboriginal communities are now examining the report. We are developing a new policy with these communities so as to respond more effectively to their very urgent needs.

Mr. Speaker, before I continue with my supplementary I should say that whatever way we cut it, there is a 10,000 housing shortfall for the aboriginal people and that is from Auditor General, not me.
My supplementary question is for the associate minister of Indian and northern affairs. Education, as she well knows, is fundamental to the future of aboriginal Canadians. The federal government is obligated to meet the educational needs of all aboriginal students.
How can the minister justify capping the funding on post-secondary education to aboriginal people and how can the government refuse 5,000 students by creating a waiting list of those 5,000 students who have made it through high school, despite great adversity and through a very high drop-out list? How can the government justify this capping of funds?

speakeroldname: Hon. Monique Landry (Minister for External Relations and Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)):
speakerposition: Minister for External Relations; Minister responsible for La Francophonie; Minister of State (Indian Affairs and Northern Development)
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I believe this government has recognized how important education is to aboriginal communities. Although the hon. member may not be aware of the fact, I am pleased to say that we have tripled the amounts provided since 1984-85, and we have almost tripled the number of students who now reach post-secondary level. We have increased our funding, and this year the budget for this category is $190 million and will increase to $242 million in 1995-96. We are also reviewing the problem that although all class I and class II spaces have been filled we realize that some students may have been left out. We will try to deal with this problem as soon as possible.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of State for Transport.
Media reports in Winnipeg suggest that the government's own CN has a plan to ship grain and potash, bypassing Thunder Bay and the seaway, through Fort Frances and Windsor through U.S. rail links. This plan, if adopted and allowed to go ahead, will mean the beginning of the end of the port at Thunder Bay, the seaway and a number of ports in the province of Quebec.
I want to ask the Minister of State for Transport: Will she instruct CN to cease and desist?

Mr. Speaker, I share my hon. friend's concern about this, but I want to reassure him that there is no plan to ship grain through the U.S.
As he says, it was speculation. It is not true that there is no shipping of grain through those ports. It will continue to flow through Thunder Bay.

I have a supplementary question for the same minister, Mr. Speaker. I know that CN denies the existence of this plan, but it has denied the existence of other plans that have come true in the past.
As the holder of the shares in this Crown corporation the Government of Canada has the right to instruct CN not to develop any plans to bypass any Canadian ports in the movement of grain, potash or any other commodities. Is the minister prepared to take the responsibility on behalf of the people of Canada?

Mr. Speaker, I take my responsibility to the people of Canada very sincerely. CN has already advised the port officials at Thunder Bay that it has no plans to do this so there is no need for me to order it.

Oral Questions

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Secretary of State, but in his absence I would like to direct it to the responsible minister. The Auditor General of Canada was very critical of the process of contracting out translation in his department. It seems that 42 per cent of current translation requests are contracted out, and that by 1994 this percentage could be as high as 50 per cent.
The quality of translation is also criticized by the Auditor General, who says that the ability of the Department of the Secretary of State to manage its human resources is poor. My question is very straightforward. Does the government intend to take action as soon as possible to deal with the problems raised by the Auditor General? Will it set clear and precise management objectives for the practice of contracting out translation? Or, is it about to dismantle the Translation Bureau and sacrifice it on the altar of privatization? That is my question.

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext: No, Mr. Speaker. We intend to keep this essential service, and it is an excellent one. Yes, we have started to take action, and I can say quite frankly that the department has accepted the recommendations and is quite pleased with them. It has already set up a task force that is to start on a complete and comprehensive review of the operations of the Translation Bureau. I am told that by next spring there will be a new plan on the basis of which a comprehensive strategy will be implemented for this service.

I have a supplementary question, Mr. Speaker.
The Auditor General has said that the contracting of translation services are badly managed. That is a serious accusation. He says that the government has lost a lot of talented employees, that the work climate is not good, that the morale is very low, and that there is a drop in the over-all quality of translations.
Canada with two official languages must have quality translation. As the percentage of translation done by the private sector is expected to rise to 50 per cent by 1994, what measures will the Secretary of State undertake to solve these problems of subcontracting translation services to people outside the Public Service of Canada?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Minister of Multiculturalism and Citizenship):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on behalf of the minister who is away on government business today, I indicated that the department agrees with the recommendations of the Auditor General. I also indicated that it has already undertaken a number of very positive measures that will definitely propose new ways of delivering the service.
As far as the morale, I think it is a group that has performed brilliantly. It has given excellent service. It does translation service in perhaps 60 languages, from what I remember in my stay with that ministry.
I think this new little team that has been doing its analysis and work has been very well seen by those members. We certainly will do everything we can to protect the service that has been in place for 57 years.

Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Minister of Transport.
Six and a half years ago the Minister of Transport stated in this House: "This government has no intention of downgrading the role of Winnipeg as a transportation centre and as an important part of the CNR".
Since that commitment was made-I use the word "commitment" loosely in this case-Manitobans have lost approximately 2,000 jobs, most of which were lost at the Transcona shops in Symington Yards.
With further reports that there could be as many as 1,300 other jobs cut throughout Canada, many which will be in Manitoba, when will CN management and this government stop bludgeoning the Manitoba rail worker?

Mr. Speaker, CN does have a mandate to act fiscally responsible and build a railroad that will continue to serve the people across this country. It has to make certain decisions in putting its fiscal plan together.
December 4, 1991

The article in the Winnipeg newspaper at this time is speculative and I do not think we should comment on it any further at this time.

Mr. Speaker, my supplementary question is for the same minister.
Four years ago the government made another commitment, this time to maintain Winnipeg as a rail transportation hub. No wonder people are nervous: all these commitments.
Since then we have seen approximately 250 rail jobs that have been lost, quite apart from the 2,000 CN jobs that I just mentioned. Some 1,000 of those jobs were lost during the last three years.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-20 is an act to amend certain statutes to implement the budget tabled in this House on February 26, 1991. Bill C-20 was introduced to imple-
Govemment Orders
ment four particular or special initiatives outlined in the February 1991 federal budget.
One of the most important changes would provide amendments to the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements and Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act and extend the cap on Established Programs Financing transfers to the provinces. What that actually means is that transfer payments from the federal government to the provinces will not increase, not even to pay the rate of inflation or the additional costs of those programs to the provinces.
The provinces are going to have to come up with the additional money to cover inflationary increases and the other increased costs related to post-secondary education and health care. That has some very serious consequences for Canadians. It also says that the federal government is walking away from its responsibility.
Another proposed amendment would dramatically increase unemployment insurance payments for both employees and employers.
The other two amendments would provide for the capping of sessional allowances and a continued freeze on tax transfers to the provinces collected from public utilities. So there is another capping by the federal government on those programs.
With Bill C-20 the government hopes to extend the freeze on those Established Programs Financing transfers for an additional three years. Imagine, for another three years, not just this year. Established Programs Financing transfer payments are made to the provinces, as I said, to support health and higher education.
It specifically means that in those two areas the provinces are going to have to come up with greater sums of money to cover the natural increases that they have to pay in administering post-secondary education and medicare even to the extent of covering the inflation rate itself. We can see where the government is going here.
How can the provinces cope? As I said yesterday, they can either cope by increasing taxation or simply cutting back on the services. The government is saying: "If you cut back on services, provinces, we are going to punish

December 4, 1991
Government Orders
you". I will get around in a moment to how that is going to take place.
We know what effect this is going to have on John Q. Public in Canada. As I said, to ensure the adherence to the standards of the Canada Health Act, the government has included a provision in this bill whereby it could withhold, reduce or deduct either money from the cash portion of the transfers or from any other transfer payments made to the provinces, not just for post-secondary education and health services. Any other services to the provinces can be deducted if the province does not maintain national standards in medicare.
The federal government is saying to the provinces: "We are not going to pay to maintain the services of medicare nationally across this country. We are going to make you, the provinces, pay for it". We know that some provinces will not be able to afford to do this.
The constitutionality of this clause, providing for the withholding of other transfers, is being challenged in the courts. A law firm reviewing the bill has suggested the bill would exceed the federal government's authority to intervene in health policy.
Going on, I just want to lay some groundwork. The former Minister of Finance gave notice in his February 19, 1991 budget that the freeze on these program entitlements announced in the 1990 budget for 1990-91 and 1991-92 would be extended to 1994-95, that is the next three years. At that time the finance minister said-and listen to this very carefully; this has been said before, but it bears repeating and repeating-"I recognize that limiting the growth of transfers under Established Programs Financing raises concerns about the ability of the federal government to continue enforcing national medicare principles under the Canada Health Act". He said that on February 26 at page 18 of his budget speech.
However, he went on to assure Canadians that "the principles of the Canada Health Act will not be compromised". Further to this pledge, the former Minister of Finance stated: "Legislation will be introduced to ensure that the federal government continues to have the means to enforce these national medicare principles". That too was said in the budget speech.
The question has to be asked here: If the federal government does not pay enough money into the national medicare scheme to pull its own weight, how does it
have the right to cal! the tune? That is precisely what is being challenged in the courts.
The Minister of Finance spoke again in February of this year. What he said is contained in clause 23(2) of Bill C-20. The beginning of that particular clause of the bill states, and I will not read all of it because to many people it will be a bunch of gobbledegook, including to myself:
In this section, "federal payment", in respect of a province, means a payment by Canada to the province under this or any other Act of Parliament or any fiscal arrangement or agreement between Canada and the province, whether enacted or entered into before or after the coming into force of this section.
That is a blanket coverage.
This legislation goes far beyond withholding any transfer fund entitlements as a means of deterring the Canada Health Act violations. Provinces within Bill C-20 have the potential to undermine the full range of federal transfer programs. In order to punish a province that does not comply to the standards laid down by the federal government, which itself is not willing to pay its own way, innocent individuals will suffer. Provincial health care practices will now have a direct bearing on child care, welfare, municipalities, aboriginal people, farmers, students and numerous other individuals and groups that stand to be denied programming that is cost shared by the federal and provincial governments. I included municipalities.
The municipalities across this country are going to be hard hit because of the lack of transfer payments from the federal government to the provinces. The provinces will have to tighten up their expenditures and will probably give less money to the municipalities to help them with their shared cost programs. The whole thing will fall at the feet of John Q. Taxpayer at the local level.
Some people will say: "Well, it is going to rest on his shoulders anyway". However, the fact remains that we have a federal government that should show leadership but it does not want to show that leadership. It is passing the burden on to the provinces and on to the municipalities across this country.
What repercussions on other items could this reduction have? It means that, in accordance with the provisions of Bill C-20, the federal government can penalize provinces that do not maintain its standard of medicare by interfering with a whole host of programs. It can take
December 4, 1991

not only from transfer payments but from other payments going to the provinces.
First, equalization payments alone are estimated to provide $8.4 billion in 1991-92 to provinces without sufficient revenues to provide reasonably comparable levels of public services at reasonably comparable levels of taxation. The federal government could deduct from that if national standards of medicare are not met in individual provinces.
Territorial financing is estimated to provide $1.41 billion for 1991-92 to the territorial governments to enable them to provide the range of public services in the north provided by provincial governments. Can you imagine those programs to the territories being cut? What base of taxation do they have to make up the difference? It is an horrendous piece of legislation that penalizes the regions of Canada, particularly those that are in greatest need.
Grants in lieu of taxes are paid to provincial and municipal governments by the federal government instead of paying taxes on federal and diplomatic property. These grants are estimated at $344 million in 1991-92. They could be deducted.
Public utilities income tax transfer payments represent 95 per cent of the federal income tax collected from certain privately owned public utilities transferred by the federal government to the provinces. This transfer is estimated at $280 million in 1991-92.
Statutory subsidies are the oldest transfer payments and are paid to each province under the terms of Confederation. These subsidies are estimated at $36 million for 1991-92.
The federal government shares the cost of each province's income maintenance and social services programs on a 50/50 basis under the Canada Assistance Act. That is important. The federal contribution for 1991-92 is estimated at $6.4 billion. In this time of recession we can imagine what it means to individual provinces and municipalities if the federal government backs off from paying its full contribution to social welfare at the local level in this country at a time when social welfare is increasing for the municipalities across this country.
Government Orders
The reeve of one municipality informed me that his welfare budget has increased by 2,000 per cent compared to what it is normally.
How can small municipalities cope with the federal government cutting its share of payments to the provinces and the provinces therefore not having enough money? At the same time the provinces have to increase taxes in order to cover post-secondary education and health costs.
What about the crop insurance contribution? In this day when the farmers of this country are going through the most horrendous times they have faced since the early thirties, or possibly in the history of Canada, can you imagine the crop insurance contributions, estimated at $207 million for 1991, possibly being cut because a province is not going to pay the federal share to keep up the cost of post-secondary education and hospital care?
There is also the Young Offenders Act, which I mentioned yesterday. There is a whole host of others but a bill went through third reading in this House last week covering the amendments to the Young Offenders Act in this country.
Under that legislation young offenders while in prison will have to receive medical treatment to assess when it is safe for them to be back out on the street. The big question in the minds of Canadians today is: Why are people who then cause other problems released prematurely? We need the medical services in those prisons to assess when it is safe for an individual to go out on the street.
The federal government is passing legislation that says to Canadians that it is going to make their streets safe and at the same time it is not providing the money to administer the program itself. That is passing the buck and it shows the lack of a responsible attitude by the national government of this country.
We know that the government is increasing the Unemployment Insurance Act by 24.4 per cent.
You are giving me the high sign, Mr. Speaker. I will abide by your ruling with one minute to go.
As I have said before in this House, the federal Government of Canada was given the responsibility for the unemployed in this nation in 1940 as an amendment to the BNA Act. That was a result of the Rowell-Sirois commission report of 1937, which was the most in-depth

Government Orders
study into poverty, economic conditions, and taxation jurisdictions between the federal and provincial governments ever made in Canadian history.
Today this government is increasing unemployment insurance rates by 24.4 per cent but it is not paying for it. It is placing the responsibility of paying for the entire program on the employer and the employee. That is not just passing the buck. That is neglecting your constitutional responsibility as the Government of Canada.
It was introduced to help those municipalities, to help those poor areas of Canada. Now this federal government is passing the buck to them and making them pay. Before this is over we must have another in-depth investigation into the tax sharing policies of this nation because the provinces and the municipalities are being put to the wall and they cannot afford it. It is up to the national government in Ottawa to show leadership on this and ensure that the transfer of taxes is carried on so that these programs are funded. Otherwise we should not have the audacity to pass the legislation in this House of Commons.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I understand that I only have 10 minutes at this point in time in the debate.
This particular bill has numerous difficulties for the constituents I represent in this Chamber. I want to outline some of those concerns.
The bill which was laid before the House some time ago is a result of trying to implement the February 1991 budget. There are a number of things this bill intends to do.
The first intention is to make amendments to the Federal-Provincial Fiscal Arrangements Act, the Federal Post-Secondary Education and Health Contributions Act, and to extend the cap on the Established Programs Financing transfers to the provinces.
Post-secondary education is of fundamental importance to a society which wishes and hopes to be internationally competitive. Many of our young people from coast to coast wish to pursue their post-secondary studies not only so that they will be qualified and their skills be enhanced but also to give them an opportunity to make a meaningful contribution to Canadian society.
The unfortunate part of this particular bill is that the transfer payment cutbacks and the capping on various payments to certain provinces have provided some very serious hardships for our students across this country. So much so that in my own constituency, in my own university, the University College of Cape Breton, students have been told by this government that any student loan they receive has 3 per cent on the front end taken from that loan.
I think I have indicated before that this amount of money to the casual observer does not look like an extensive amount of money. However, if you are taking 3 per cent of $3,000 it is rather sizeable in terms of what students can purchase with that money, whether it is supplies for their particular class, transportation to and from the university or transportation from the university to their own homes if they should happen to live outside that particular province or that particular area. It is a tax on young people who are trying to acquire a post-secondary education.
It is somewhat hypocritical of the government to say that on the one hand it wants to have meaningful consultations concerning competitiveness, as it said in the prosperity document tabled by the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce. Students really are- and I do not wish to flatter their egos unduly but the fact remains-our best hope. Young people are our best hope for the future in terms of what they can do to improve Canadian society. I think that Bill C-20 acts to impede the progress of students and of young people, particularly as it relates to post-secondary education.
The government will say, and say quite rightly: "Well, we are still giving an increase in the amount of money going to universities". However, what if you were anticipating a certain level of increase and guaranteed that particular increase and then someone came along and said: "I am sorry, it is going to have to be x minus y, that is what you're going to get"? That throws budgets of provincial governments off and certainly has a negative effect on the administration of universities, whether in terms of providing research moneys for professors, providing facilities to needy students, or the actual fact that some individuals will have to lose their jobs as a result. There is only so much money in the pot.
December 4, 1991	COMMONS
Education is one thing and post-secondary education is very, very important. However, Bill C-20 goes on to talk about health in the respective provinces. There is a certain pot of money made available to provincial governments in have not provinces such as Nova Scotia to carry on and implement the principles of the Canada Health Act. Any time money is taken out of that pot, it directly affects the prospects of the health care system.
What do I mean? I mean that there will probably be less money for research. However, if there is not to be less money for research and health care they will steal it somewhere else. Sometimes it is felt not by the medical doctors but by people such as the janitor who works in the hospital. I know many janitors who work in hospitals, whether in Glace Bay, New Waterford in my constituency, Sydney or Sydney River. They are the ones who will feel the effects because lay-offs will have to occur and overtime will be curbed. They are the ones on the health care scale who will, in effect, be cheated as a result of Bill C-20. I do not think any of us in this Chamber can overlook the fact that these cutbacks, as announced by the government through Bill C-20 and its February budget of 1991, will have traumatic effects on what Canadians believe is the most important social program ever put in place.
I have tremendous difficulty with the attempt of members opposite to erode the fundamentals of medicare. I know government members will say they are not doing that. They say there is no way they are not eroding the fundamentals of medicare. But remember the pie and all the services in the pie. When you shrink the pie, something has to happen to research or the maintenance provided in the various hospitals. That is what happens.
Bill C-20 also goes on about unemployment insurance premiums. In the few minutes I have left, I want to tell the Chair that I have never seen such hypocrisy by a government, as demonstrated in Bill C-20, as it affects the UIC premiums.
Let us not forget that the hon. member for St. John's West, in the last federal election, stated on national television that there would be no changes to the unemployment insurance program in this country. Now, under the auspices of Bill C-20, we have an increase in UIC premiums of 24.4 per cent.

Government Orders
Some commitment, some promise by members opposite. It will affect the average working Canadian and the average employer in the various small businesses across this country. Some of them do not have huge profits like General Motors or some of the major corporations in this country to pay this additional tax. Some of them are operating from week to week, from month to month. It is the individual who runs the dry cleaning store, the pizza shop or drug store who is going to feel the negative effects of the increase in the UIC premiums. It is so unfair. It is hypocrisy at its worst. The Minister of Finance, when I questioned him, would not be candid enough to indicate there would be no increases in 1992. Now we are going to have more of an increase, not just 24 per cent but more than that.
In conclusion, I thank you for the opportunity to make this intervention. I hope hon. members opposite will see their way to vote down the provisions of Bill C-20, which is a Draconian piece of legislation. I am sure the hon. minister would want to agree with me, only for the provisions of cabinet solidarity.

Mr. Speaker, in the brief time I have for my remarks today, I would first of all like to refer to Bill C-20 and what it means to the provinces of Canada, the people within the province of British Columbia, my home province, and my riding of Okanagan- Similkameen-Merritt.
Bill C-20 is a continuation of Bill C-69 which was so drastic in its cutbacks to post-secondary education and health care delivery to Canada and the provinces, but in particular to the province of British Columbia.
This particular bill continues until fiscal year 1994-95 the cutbacks to the Established Programs Financing, those transfers to the provinces for post-secondary education and health care within those provinces.
Over that period of time, as I understand it, the cuts amount to almost $9.5 billion. They will cost the province of British Columbia over that period of time almost $1.2 billion.
That money has to come from somewhere. We either cut back on our programs, or we have to increase taxes within our separate provinces or municipalities.

December 4, 1991

I have heard through letters from my constituents and discussions with other members from all sides of the House that this particular bill, the continuation of Bill C-69 and Bill C-20, is the commencement of the death of medicare as we know it.
Certainly members on the other side of the House may say that we are being alarmist and are trying to scare people. I think it is about time the people of Canada realized they have to wake up and ensure that this government is not elected again.
It has continued on the path it has taken over the last years since it was first elected in 1984. Now we see the erosion of our education programs, our health care system and life as we know it in Canada. I think we have to become somewhat alarmed. We have to start speaking out.

The people of Canada will not stand for the continued erosion and attack on these programs. My parents and their parents fought for them over the years and the young people of Canada take them for granted as part of what makes up Canada.
The riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt has triple the percentage of senior's population as does the rest of Canada. Almost 33 per cent of the residents of Okanagan-Similkameen, certain areas in the Okanagan Valley and to some extent the boundary country and Similkameen Valley, are over 65 years of age.
If you look at the retirement population, that figure jumps to almost 50 per cent of the population.
How does this bill, the cutbacks in the transfer payments and Established Programs Financing in the area of health care alone, affect my area? It is devastating. This bill in its substance is looked on by the people of my riding and myself as a Draconian measure. It can only continue to hurt those who need to be assisted the most such as those with lower and middle incomes, and those on fixed incomes such as the seniors in my area.
I am alarmed. I am very upset at the prospect that the people in my riding, in British Columbia and across Canada are going to be so devastated by the terms and direction this bill is taking Canada and our health care system.
I have heard many problems from people coming to me over the last six months to a year. In one case a woman in Oliver, British Columbia said her husband has been on a medical waiting list to have a necessary knee operation, but he cannot get into the hospital because of the cutbacks in the care. He is not a priority and yet this gentleman is crippled. He is unable to work. They have an orchard, and his wife must do the orchard work. They are not a young couple, yet they are being penalized by the terms and conditions set out by this government with the cutbacks in the health care systems.
I would also like to talk about the cutbacks in post-secondary education. In my riding there are three colleges: Selkirk College, of which I am an alumnus; Okanagan College, which is central to the Okanagan Valley; and Caribou College which goes into the Merritt region.
Those areas are directly affected. As the cost of post-secondary education increases, it becomes increasingly more difficult for the average Canadian, the average wage earner, to assist their children, daughters and sons, to go on to university. Universities and colleges are forced to increase fees substantially. The costs of books, room and board and transportation continue to rise under the policies of this government.
We try to encourage our young people to get their education in our region where it is slightly cheaper. Yet by doing this, we are forcing those young people out of post-secondary education and into the job market.
Unfortunately, because of the policies of this government, there have also been cutbacks in the Canada Assistance Plan and cutbacks are probable in the area of welfare.
In order to get unemployment insurance, the students have to work longer periods of time. Because their qualification period is longer, their benefit period has been shortened. It is difficult to get jobs in areas like the Okanagan, where the rate of unemployment is substantially higher than the national average. In Merritt, for instance, in the last couple of years the rate of unemployment has increased to something like 34 per cent. I just heard this week that one of the major employers in
December 4, 1991

the city of Merritt, one of the major sawmills, has laid off a number of employees. They could be laid off from one month to four months or perhaps longer.
They lay the blame on the fiscal and monetary policies of this government-the GST and the problems that it has caused. They lay the blame on the differences in the extra taxation through unemployment insurance premiums. Mr. Speaker, I want to thank my hon. friend from Burin-St. George's. He launched into the stern end of his speech, as we would say, on a subject that I had not planned to speak on. Since he was cut off, and rightly so of course, I want to elaborate on his emotion and his concern with the unemployment insurance aspect of what this bill stands for. Just to refresh our minds, one of the things Bill C-20 will do is increase unemployment insurance payments for both the employers and the employees.
We have to go back and check the history of unemployment insurance. I do not want to go back to 1940 when the Liberals introduced this as a safety net for Canadians who would be out of work. I want to go back four years. At that time unemployment insurance worked this way: the government paid 26 per cent, the employee paid 31 per cent and the employer paid 40 per cent more than the employee and that worked out to 43 per cent.
A few weeks before the election was called I recall that the Prime Minister and hon. Minister of Fisheries and Oceans, in response to concern that the UIC business would be changed because of the level playing field and the free trade agreement, categorically denied that it would be changed, leaving no room for concern, leaving no room for doubt.
People were telling me: "Look, did you hear what these people say? Don't go around being a fear-monger and creating doubt in people's minds". I had some doubt myself on this occasion, but six months later the hon.
Government Orders
Minister of Employment and Immigration introduced measures that eventually led to Bill C-21. Then all my doubts were certainly removed that the level playing field was about to be launched.
One week before the general election-and this is factual-the government cut UI payments by 17 per cent and raised benefits by 7 per cent, denying that the timing of this had anything to do with the impending federal vote. Weekly earnings dropped from $2.35 for each $100 of insurable earnings down to $1.95 the week before the election. Six months after the election Bill C-21 was introduced which took the government entirely out of the unemployment insurance business.
In other words, it has contributed 26 per cent to look after the administration of the fund and to make sure that the money was always there to pay and that people would not have to have their premiums raised. It got out of the whole business. The government does not now contribute.
What has happened? As a result the 1989 budget, not long after the election, increased the employee premiums back to where they were, by about a 10-cent difference back to $2.25 for the employee for $100 of insurable earnings. I will just stick with the employee because the employer went up accordingly. Consistent with the provision of the labour force development strategy which later became Bill C-21, the budget iterated-this is the budget of 1989-that the government would now not contribute to the plan.
In the next budget that concerned unemployment insurance, the budget we are discussing here today, Bill C-20, The Budget Papers-and I just read them-stated in part: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums".
If the times have been harder economically to the people I represent-and I know a lot of people are represented on this side of the House-I do not know when they could be any worse. The government is going back on its word. It has raised them from $2.25 to $2.80. Now they are going to be raised again.
Even before the budget is approved and formal approval is given for something that happened on July 1 that is raising the UIC rates by 24 per cent, and even as

Government Orders
we debate it in the House today, on January 1 it is going to be raised another 7.1 per cent.
I am not sure how we could look at that as any kind of a promise that was kept. In fact I think it is the reverse. It is a promise that has been broken on three separate occasions. It is broken by the trust that if times are rough you will not have to pay the premium. That is exactly what it said.
What does this mean? The latest one, which we are not discussing today and which we will have to discuss some other time, means a tax increase of $204 a year for somebody earning $40,000. For the average person in my riding it is going to cost them between $60 and $95 a year. Mr. Speaker, you may say that is not very much. It is a lot when you do not have the money.
I do not know where we are heading with this, quite frankly. I have spoken on the dreadful effect, not that it is going to have but that it already has on health care. I have a lot of seniors in my riding. They have enough to worry about. This is a concern that has gone through every one of the almost 70 seniors homes in my riding. In the last year I have visited them all.
Turning to post-secondary education, most of us have spoken to students in schools. We see them on a regular basis. I write to them and get a lot of letters from them. They are concerned about the apparent lack of financing that is going to take place when this bill is passed.
I do not live in a dream world. I hope that very few of us do in this House. I know that money does not grow on trees. I know that the country is in trouble. We are broke. The Conservatives have been trying to pull us out of this deficit. I am not going to mention with substance that they blame it on the Liberals, but they do and that is unfortunate. After seven years in power I think it is going to be very difficult to blame another government in power seven years ago.
It is like taking over a ship and after a year you have been captain running it aground and you blame it on the previous skipper because he did not have the engine set up properly. Nobody would believe that and nobody believes the Tories when they say that we are responsible for the debt doubling by two and a half times, at least.
Those three concerns are the ones that concern me the most. The money can be found in other places. There is enough flexibility. We know how the government finances its expenditures. It can be found in some other discretionary funding. Perhaps they will have to nickel and dime it. I am not a nickel and dime person, quite frankly. I do not like doing it because it is symptomatic of other problems. Time does not permit me to get into that.
It is these three areas. Unemployment insurance has increased 54 per cent since this government came to power in 1988. That is double. There is the eventual removal of our medicare system. We have just started the first chip at the block. It is going to be chipped away. I pointed out to the House yesterday that if things keep going the way they are by the year 2000 there will not be any money left for medicare. The third one is cutting off our nose to spite our face by reducing the funding to the provinces for post-secondary education. It may in the short term save us money, but in the long term it is going to make us less competitive and put us in a position where it is going to be more difficult to prevent us from sleep walking into extinction.
I believe that is what is happening right now. I do not like it. I am concerned about it. I hope the expressions of my concern are not seen as just a partisan belief or a chance at government bashing. If I have established any reputation I think it is one for not so doing.
I do not like what is happening in this bill. I know my colleagues do not like it. I hope that there will still be some chance for a reprieve. We are through report stage. I appreciate that, but certainly when this bill comes up for passage in the near future I can assure you that it will not get my vote. I do not think we are doing the proper things to keep the country on an even keel and to look after the poorer people, the common man and the common woman. We are giving them another tax on top of the GST and 30 other taxes. I believe there has to be an alternative.

Mr. Speaker, it is kind of routine to rise in this House and say something to the effect that it is a pleasure to speak on Bill C-20. However it is not. I am tired of having to speak to bills like Bills C-96, C-69 and now C-20. It is really quite bizarre, if not hypocritical, that I left a meeting of the committee on industry, science and technology where the Minister of Industry, Science and Technology is defending the government's prosperity through competitiveness agenda which focuses, as I think you know,

on the importance of science and technology and education and training in Canada's economic survival.
After seven years in which this government has continually cut back on training, on education and R and D, suddenly the government has awakened to the fact and wants to awaken the people to the fact that the priorities for future economic development in R and D and education and so on must be seen by them to be a priority in spite of the failure of this government itself to recognize these as priorities.
I really want to focus on the issue of post-secondary education, but let us look at what the government members say in this prosperity agenda. They say that they want to eliminate illiteracy in the country. They want to quadruple the number of trainees produced in industry, but most significantly in the context of this debate they say they want to double the number of scientists, engineers and mathematicians that our university system produces.
Yet this is a government that has followed in the trail of the Liberals in producing legislation that has been subject to debate in this House, covered in Bill C-96 and Bill C-69 and now Bill C-20, which will lead to an accumulated cut of $9 billion to the post-secondary education system.
As I said they were not pioneers in the field. We will recall the changes made by the Liberal governments between 1977 and 1984 which themselves led to a bleeding from the post-secondary education system of $5.7 billion.
As we are now trying to address the whole question of how Canada's international competitiveness can be improved, we are left with the legacy of the previous government and the actions of this government continued in Bill C-20. The effect already has been catastrophic. Yet they have nerve enough to go round this country talking to people, trying to convince people that they should understand the significance of training and education, when this government utterly failed to act in respect to education in spite of its great importance.
Government Orders
The impact has been tremendously severe. It has affected accessibility. It has affected quality. It has affected costs as these costs have had to be picked up by students and faculty in the various provincial post-secondary educational systems.
Let us look at the example of Newfoundland where its single university, Memorial University, has had to cut its budget as a result of this government's actions by $10 million. It has increased tuition by 5 per cent and it has cut 100 employees.
Along with what this government has done with the challenge program and the student loans program, we have a situation at the University of Alberta where the tuition for the last two years has increased by 35 per cent. They now have there food banks for graduate students. This is because of the failure of this government to recognize that even in the context of a deficit there are spending choices that can and must be made. One of the priorities that should have been recognized by this government was expenditure in order to improve the capacity of our people to bring their knowledge, their training and their skills to the economy to make Canada more prosperous, because its people were more capable of exercising their talents.
The deficit has been used as the excuse when in fact the deficit is a function and a reflection of the deteriorating economy of this country and the failure of this government and previous governments to recognize what must be done to ensure that we have products we could sell to other nations and to our own people in competition with what is imported into our country.
Bill C-20 is another example of failure. It is an example of hypocrisy. Even now as we are moving to cut financing of post-secondary education, we have the minister down the hall saying that Canadians must recognize the priorities that this government and people must have if we are to become competitive. It will cut $9 billion from post-secondary education.
What the minister said and what this government has been doing for the last seven years is unparalled in the history of Canada. I do not know whether it is unparalled in the strict sense. It is unparalled in its failure to have actions match words. It is unparalled in the destruction

Government Orders
that has already been brought to bear on this country's capacity to survive economically and indeed politically.
Bill C-20 is another sign that this government does not know what it is doing. It will never learn and should be cast out of office.
