Mr. Speaker, I take this opportunity today to discuss the effect Bill C-20 has on one aspect only. That is the health care system of Canada.
Much of what I intend to say I have borrowed from very succinct and very well researched articles by Carol Goar of The Toronto Star. I certainly recommend this series of articles to my friends across the aisle, particularly to the minister of health. They are well research and very informative articles.
I have listened to the debates on the issue carefully and must confess that I am dismayed at what I have been hearing. I am particularly upset with this government for being so short-sighted in its approach in failing to provide the leadership to ensure that we retain an effective public health care system for all Canadians.
It seems to equate effective public health with dollars. What we have heard is if this government loosened the purse strings or gave the provinces what they wanted, our health care system would be automatically fixed. We all know that this is simply not correct.
Even if all financial constraints were lifted today, our health care system in Canada would still be in some difficulty.
We have just celebrated the 30th birthday of Canada's health care system. It is one of the best in the world. Canadians do not have to face the prospects of financial ruin should they get sick. Being poor in Canada does not deny you from being treated by a doctor or being admitted to any hospital. We can all be proud of the rigid standard of care to which most health professionals are committed.
In the last 30 years, provincially and federally, with a constantly expanding economy, governments mostly did not question the growth of the cost of the medical care system. Today we find this experience of the last 30 years can no longer continue. This government and every province are faced with increasing deficits. The deficit of this government continues to be in the neighbourhood of
$30 billion. Our national debt now far exceeds $400 billion.
Thirty-seven cents of every tax dollar collected in Canada today does not pay for one doctor's visit, does not pay for one medical procedure; 37 cents does not pay for one drug administered, does not pay for one hour of nursing care or does not pay for the use of one hospital bed. Out of every dollar collected, 37 cents goes to pay the interest on the national debt. That means we have 63 cents remaining to administer to the affairs of this total country. Health care, as we all know, takes a substantial amount of the balance.
What I am trying to get at is what we have to do and what this government must do to try and find a new way. That is where this government has failed. We must begin to restructure our health care system and this again is where this government has failed. We must develop a comprehensive national strategy and again this government has failed to do that.
A government cannot unilaterally cut health care costs in this country, as it is trying to do with the legislation that is before this House today. A federal government must take the lead with its counterparts in the provinces and the municipalities to bring into line and to bring into focus the competing bureaucracies, federally, provincially and municipally, all that are involved in the health care system.
A good federal government must take the lead to define what a health care system truly is. Remove those social programs that have become a financial albatross around the necks of the health delivery system and we should take health related matters right out of the health budget so that we can truly define what it is.
A good federal government must take the lead to be rigorous in assessment, to prove the value of new technologies, to prove the value of expensive drugs and other costly health procedures.
A federal government must take the lead to monitor carefully treatments that may be done in homes of Canadians or clinics rather than the use of expensive hospital beds.
A federal government must take the lead to establish systems that monitor Canadians who have preventable diseases so that they can find out what these diseases
December 4, 1991

are. They can no longer be ignored until they reach the expensive crisis stage for treatment.
A federal government must take the lead to monitor national services in each community so that there are no longer any expensive duplications in the delivery of health services. Long-term joint planning is an absolute
necessity.
A good federal government must take the lead to make the moral and ethical decisions as to what will be allowed by way of delivery of health care to all of our citizens.
A federal government must take the lead to advise all Canadians that user fees will not be tolerated anywhere in Canada. In this way, assure all Canadians, especially seniors and the poor, those less fortunate, that they should never have to worry about the extra costs associated with ill health.
A federal government must take the lead to renew the health system from within, using those invaluable human resources we already have within our health care system.
A federal government must lead the way in all these important areas, working in close co-operation with the provinces and the municipalities, all which are already involved in the very important health care field. We need a government that is willing to make difficult decisions necessary to bring discipline to the system of the delivery of health care in Canada. Only then, only once we have made those strong and bold decisions, can we retain our health care system. We can then not only retain our health care system but strengthen it and make it stronger than it is today for ourselves and for all future Canadians.
A Liberal government is committed to the principles I have set out in this short essay. The cutting of transfer payments is not the way to do it and this government should be embarrassed for thinking that it is.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure to engage in debate at this stage of this bill. My hon. colleague opposite has spoken quite eloquently in consideration of the provisions that are put forward.
We in the Liberal Party are extremely concerned about the erosion of federal transfers to the provinces in this country. We are extremely concerned that the government is seriously affecting the ability of provinces right across this nation to be able to provide services of national standard no matter what the wealth position of the particular province is on a given day, or a given

month, or a given year. We are very concerned that the government through its actions and through some of it own fiscal mismanagement has transferred the burden of its debt down to the poorest of the poor.
The problem that we have is that at some point freezes, cuts, and holdbacks from programs always have the effect of hurting the people that least can afford to bear the burden of that hurt. One of the big concerns we do have is the effect of the cuts to Established Programs Financing. The cuts to Established Programs Financing in this country have been absolutely awesome over the last few years.
The government has initiated a freeze on transfers to the provinces under EPF. The government at the same point in time will indicate that it is fulfilling its commitment under the Constitution Act to provide for equalization payments and to ensure that equalization payments are sufficient to allow every single province in this country to be able to deliver programs of national standards.
The effects on the freezes on EPFs that this government has undertaken have been absolutely dramatic. When we were studying another bill at pre-study, Bill C-22, the Bankruptcy Act, we had a submission put to us by the Canadian Hospital Association. The Canadian Hospital Association presented us with a brief and I indicated to them at that time that the particular brief may not be that appropriate for the bill we were studying at pre-study, Bill C-22, but I certainly knew that it had a great deal of relevancy and that it would be debated and that I wanted to quote it in this particular place.
The erosion of health care, the erosion of the ability of every province to have universities of national standards, the ability of each and every province to be able to deliver health care of national standards has been severely threatened by this government.
If you look at the effect of EPF savings over what was anticipated with the regular growth of EPFs, the dollar amounts are startling. Between 1986 and 1996 the federal government will have saved $29,998 billion. Nearly $30 billion it has cut from the anticipated transfers to the provinces for health care.
That is shameful, Mr. Speaker. This is at the same time, if you look at it, that provinces like Newfoundland, Nova Scotia, or for goodness' sakes provinces like Saskatchewan, have not seen their lot in Confederation get any better. In actual fact, in relative terms, their

Government Orders
disparity against the national average economically is getting worse.
Instead of recognizing that the federal government has a responsibility to ensure that transfers to the provinces are sufficient to meet that objective in our Constitution Act, that equalization payments shall occur to ensure the programs of national standards are able to be maintained, what does it do during this period of decline in the poorest of the poor provinces? It cuts back.
It is not as easy as the government would have us believe, that it can walk forward and can say easily: "Well, Nova Scotia, we have cut back on what you expected us to transfer for health care. You will have to make it up somewhere else". "Newfoundland, look we are sorry about this but we cannot give you as much, but you are still supposed to be able to deliver the same standard of health care to your people as was provided by the Government of Ontario, or the Government of Quebec, or the Government of Alberta". Thirty billion dollars cut because of freezes on EPFs.
The health care system in Canada is in peril. Provincial governments who want to ensure that universality of health care is maintained in their jurisdictions have been put against the wall. What are they to do?
In a period of 10 short years the federal government has deprived the provinces of Canada of $30 billion that was to go toward the delivery of health care services. Just a few weeks ago the Conservatives got up on their hind feet, bayed at the moon and said: "We are going to talk about prosperity. We are going to inflict prosperity on the country with new initiatives". Their new boondoggle was to go around and consult Canadians about prosperity-
Anybody who has an ounce of sense in their head knows that the prosperity and competitiveness of any nation is directly linked to the quality and level of education provided to its citizens. When a country decides that it does not have the money to invest in education for its young then five or ten years down the road you will see a decline in the competitiveness of that
nation, a decline in the per capita output, and a decline in the quality of life in that country.
The government likes to talk a good deal about inflicting prosperity. That is its latest buzzword. The facts are that the cutbacks this government has undertaken between 1986 and 1996 will see $12,109 billion cut in the transfers to the provinces that allow every province across this country to have affordable post-secondary education of national standard.
This government's 1986 to 1996 program of cutbacks has ensured that education and the dream of a post-secondary education has become a dream that only the wealthy in this country can afford. That is what this government has done.
Nova Scotia is not a rich province but we have a heck of a lot of resolve down there. We have some of the finest universities in Canada, and they have been there for a long time. My colleague from Saskatoon who taught at one of those universities knows that is the case. I think he taught at Saint Mary's University. In the good old days at Saint Mary's University, the students could come and get a small student loan and know they could get a quality education. The tuitions have had to go through the roof.
At Dalhousie University, just down the road from Saint Mary's in Halifax, the students basically had to barge in and occupy the senate building while the administration of the university was trying to figure out how to grapple with rising costs because it is not getting the money from the federal government.
As much as I am concerned about health care, I know that this government will use every single opportunity it can get its hands on to cut those essential transfers to provinces, the lifeblood of many of these provinces, allowing them to maintain programs of national standard.
The government says: "We are concerned about medicare". If it is so concerned about medicare and about whether or not there are going to be user fees in Nova Scotia and New Brunswick it should not come in with punitive legislation that will allow the government to walk in and withhold funds in other areas in which it has already cut back. If the government is truly interested it should not be introducing Draconian legislation like we currently have before us and are debating. If the govern-
December 4, 1991

ment is truly concerned about the erosion of health care in Canada it should not seek to penalize those provinces it has driven to the brink as a result of its cutbacks.
The Conservatives should recognize that they are the authors of Canada's misfortune in our health care field, not the provinces. They should remove the freeze on EPF funding that they themselves have imposed. It is that freeze, not the provinces, that has jeopardized the universal medicare program a Liberal government introduced and which has served this countiy so well.

Mr. Speaker, I am not going to say that it is a pleasure for me to take part in this debate because it is not.
I feel obligated because what we are discussing here today is yet another characteristic of the present Conservative government and its determination to further erode the fiscal arrangements between the federal Government of Canada and the various provinces.
Bill C-20 is really a bill to transfer debt, not payments, from the federal government to the provincial governments in this country. Then the provincial governments are forced to pass on that debt and that debt burden to the municipalities.
Now, instead of the federal Government of Canada assuming its debt responsibilities here in Ottawa, the buck stops at the council chamber of the various cities, towns and villages across this country.
It is manifestly unfair and dangerous that we should be engaged in this kind of buck passing from the federal level to the provincial and the municipal levels. The people at the municipal level may not be able to understand or conceive of billions of dollars but can certainly understand, conceive of and appreciate cutbacks in the realm of hundreds of thousands of dollars as seen at their level.
First, I would like to point out that we are not curing any of our economic ills, problems and challenges in this country by passing debt from the federal government to the provincial governments, and they in turn to the municipal governments.
Second, it is absolutely disgraceful that a federal government should continue to cut back on the amounts of money it passes on to the provinces for the specific purpose of post-secondary education.
Government Orders
It is a well-known fact that the best universities in our country today are suffering badly from a lack of funding. It is a well-known fact that our libraries, research facilities, teaching capabilities and our learning environments across this country are suffering from a lack of proper funding.
That means that not only are our universities not living up to world-class status but various faculties and departments within universities are losing their world-class status. I am referring to such eminent universities as the University of Toronto, McGill University, Queen's and so on.
This is not a criticism of the academic capability of the teachers and students in those institutions. However, it is a fact that all institutions of higher learning in our country are suffering as a result of a very unwise policy on the part of this federal Conservative government to cut back in that area which we should be pumping more funds into, namely the research and development that industry and commerce will need in this country if we are to survive in this increasingly competitive world.
We have to make certain that more money is pumped into research, not only research and development but in skills, training and basic educational upgrading.
I represent a constituency that has been severely hurt by this recession. Yet when I look at the number of persons drawing unemployment insurance I see that the proportion of those on UI today simply drawing unemployment insurance and not in training or retraining programs is exactly the same as in 1981-82.
It has not changed one iota. We have not improved the retraining and upgrading of skills during this recession compared to 10 years ago in the 1981-82 recession. In other words, this government has not learned anything.
It talks about competitiveness and it talks about globalization, yet it is not prepared to make a concerted effort to improve the funding for research and development on the corporate side or improve the amount of funding going into job skills, job training and basic elementary educational upgrading on the worker side, the so-called adjustment side. This comes at a time when we are suffering not only from a severe recession but from all the strains and stresses brought upon us by the free trade agreement with the United States, which will be made worse if that trade agreement is expanded to include Mexico. That also is an area in which this government has been most unwise and injudicious in its

Government Orders
spending practices virtually since 1984, but certainly the last couple of years.
Finally, the issue of medicare has been raised by speaker after speaker on this side. Nobody is getting up on the other side to defend the government's position on cutbacks to the provinces that will adversely affect medicare in this country, but certainly speakers on this side of the House have mentioned it time and time again, today and in previous days during this debate.
The Canadian medicare system is undergoing stress and is having problems, not all of which are financially based but a great proportion is financially based. We fail to understand the vision that brought in medicare, not just the dollars and cents, but the vision behind medicare. Medicare was originally conceived as not just a humanitarian approach to helping the ill and curing the sick but as a concerted, philosophical effort on the part of previous governments to make certain that all Canadian citizens, regardless of income or social position, regardless of what assets they might possess, had equal access to the very best medical treatment this country had to offer.
That is a basic moral and philosophical commitment this government has forgotten. This government is looking at medicare through the eyes of an accountant and an accountant only, not through the eyes of those of us who look upon medicare as one of the foundations of social policy in this country.
When you lose sight of the moral and philosophical aspect of medicare it is very easy to sit back with an accountant's pen and, over a very short period of time, maybe three, four or five years, see medicare disappear as a social medical program. Before we know it we are going to have user fees. We are going to have all kinds of added costs to our medicare system that will eventually return us to the system I recall from the 1950s when if you had money you had the operation but if you did not have the money or asset you could not have the operation.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a privilege to speak again on this bill now that it has been through committee and is back in the House. This is a bill that demonstrates the fundamental approach being taken by the current government to this country which is contrary to our whole history, contrary to the sense of sharing and creating equal opportunities for all Canadians which has been our tradition since its founding.
I want to speak briefly about some of the programs that are going to be seriously damaged by this bill. I want to start with the fundamental principle that I think should apply when we look at programs like education, medicare, unemployment insurance, young offenders services, the general sharing of revenues between the federal and provincial governments and down to the municipal and community life of this country.
The fundamental principle which this government likes to tout and talk about, but seems to have a great deal of trouble actually respecting when it comes to implementing legislation, is the simple statement that our most important resource as a nation is our people. I have heard that often from the government benches.
December 4, 1991

Every time I see legislation, it is legislation that ignores that principle entirely. Let me touch on some of the principles of this bill that I think do that.
Fundamentally, if we believe that people should have an opportunity to develop the best of their talents and make a contribution to Canada and if we believe in a society where every citizen should have the capacity to develop to the best they can be, we believe in education.
If we believe that we are facing an increasingly global competitive situation that Canada must be part of internationally, then surely we believe in education at the post-secondary level for any citizen who is capable of achieving the standard to achieve a higher education.
What does this bill do? It says that the federal Government of Canada, the government with the responsibility for the ability of this country to compete internationally in a new world where knowledge is going to become at least as and probably more important than resources, is going to cap its contribution to post-secondary education in Canada. That means we are going to continue four more years the cap on the ability to develop and use the talents of all young Canadian people. It means a cap on the ability of people in mid-career who find they have to shift the direction of their career and training. It means stopping their ability to return to university, to be able to adapt to the changing economy and the changing world environment the government is so fond of preaching about.
If we need one concrete example, I need only refer to a statement from the Siemens Corporation, which is hoping to create 3,000 new jobs in Canada in the next short while. The main reason it may decide not to do that is because it is not sure it can get the qualified people. However, this government wants to cap its spending on education.
It wants to put a cap on social services. We have all heard numerous times in this House the statistics about poverty and what poverty ends up costing us if we do not deal with the poverty of children. We know that children living in poverty are four times as likely as the general population to drop out of high school, to never complete high school and therefore never to have the same employment opportunities, the same opportunities to contribute to the Canadian economy, as children who do complete high school and perhaps go on to university.
Government Orders
With this bill the government is ensuring that the ability of Canadian provinces and Canadian communities to deal with the issue of the poverty of one million children in this country is capped. It is capping our ability to deal with the poverty of children who are more likely to be seriously injured, more likely to die, more likely to commit suicide because of poverty.
It is not good for the health of this country that children and families live in poverty. Yet this government is saying: "We are not prepared to share the resources of this nation to solve the problems of poverty and to let young children grow up into adults who can participate and make a full contribution to Canadian society".
At a time when small businesses are experiencing bankruptcies at a highly elevated rate, and I remind the government that small businesses create 80 per cent of the new employment in this country, 80 per cent; at a time when we need employment and we need small businesses to create those jobs, this government is increasing by 24 per cent the unemployment insurance premiums, having said less than two years ago that the unemployment insurance premiums were fixed and would not change for three years.
I hope we will remember that it was only two short years ago that there was a substantial and damaging increase in unemployment insurance premiums. Only two years ago, at the same time that the GST was going to be hitting small businesses, they were also hit with an increase in unemployment insurance premiums, not to mention employees and workers in this country who are paying higher premiums for less coverage. What other provider of services in Canada could get away with that, pay us more but get less?
My final and major concern is about medicare in this country. We have a medicare system that provides health care at 25 per cent less than the cost it is provided in the United States, where it is a private health care system; 25 per cent less. We have a population that is healthier, a population that has more access to affordable health care for 25 per cent more than the cost to the United States, just to the south.

December 4, 1991
Government Orders
Yet this government wants to cut its transfer payments to support medicare to the point where the federal government will transfer no money to support a national health care system that has given us a strong and healthy population. Not only that, but it introduces a blackmail clause saying that when we are no longer paying out money for medicare to the provinces, we will take back money from services to young offenders, and from official language education at a time when national unity is a major concern. What a ridiculous thing to be even contemplating.
The blackmail clause on medicare is especially insidious, quite likely unconstitutional, and yet this government persists in saying "we will undermine the medicare system for the sake of short-term goals" that are more motivated I believe by politics than by good policy.
A great deal more time would be necessary to speak to all the failures of this bill and all the weaknesses but a diminution of looking after our primary resource, our people, is not a productive and helpful thing to do when our economy is already faltering, when we are far from out of a recession and when what we need to be is more capable, more productive, better educated and healthier.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not a happy moment for me to have to get up and speak on Bill C-20. This piece of legislation, I feel, is a pretentious omen of things to come from this government.
It is a bad piece of legislation. It has extremely harmful ramifications for Canada's social programs, extremely harmful ramifications for the future of our educational systems in Canada.
It is through the bill the government is signalling its determination to destroy Canadian institutions and essentially a Canadian way of life. The bill is essentially a signal of the beginning of the end for Canada's universal medicare system as we know it today and a slow but inevitable erosion of the federal commitment to our post-secondary education programs across this country.
Health care, post-secondary education, the unemployment insurance program, to name a few, are the victims in this bill, the victims of a Tory corporate agenda, a continued and unrelenting attack on our basic social structure in Canada and a harmonization of a style of government that becomes more and more familiar to us
as a pale copy of a market driven system that is present in our neighbour to the south.
The capping of the federal contribution to education through the legislation, capping the Established Programs Financing funding to education, is essentially a betrayal of our young people in Canada, a betrayal of their future. It is forcing students to mortgage their own futures in order to obtain their futures.
At the same time this government continually speaks of the need for international competitiveness, of a trained labour force, and at the same time it is doing that it is chipping away at the very foundation whereupon that competitiveness can be built. Unless we have a highly skilled and highly educated work force, Canada can never hope to be competitive in this global economy. At the same time that it talks about this need for global competitiveness, it erodes the very foundation of our post-secondary education system in Canada. It is getting more and more and more expensive for a student to obtain a post-secondary education in Canada today. It is becoming essentially an opportunity for those who are better off in Canada, but certainly not an opportunity for students who maybe through their own recourse do not have the financial capability of obtaining their education.
The government has claimed that it has to cut back on these programs, on the delivery of health care services to the provinces, on the delivery of funding for post-secondary education. It has to withdraw or cancel its funding from the unemployment insurance program because it claims that the cupboard is bare. That is the message that has been repeated time and time again: "The cupboard is bare". Yet, by the government's own admission, it has suddenly found over $8 billion in unpaid corporate taxes in this country in tax deferments. We see $53 million that the government has squandered on a high-tech on-line communications service through the Ministry of External Affairs to the embassies throughout the world, a service that is redundant before it has even been brought on line, a service that is still not working. There was $53 million squandered on that particular program.
We see a government that has found funding, and legitimate funding I might add, for employment opportunities in Quebec, and yet at the same time sits on its hands when jobs are lost in my home province of British Columbia, completely ignoring the plight of the forestry industry in British Columbia and ignoring the plight of our fishermen on the west coast and in the Atlantic fishery. People wonder about the equity and the fairness when the government claims the cupboard is bare and yet finds these funds and finds the $8 billion that it has simply ignored and refused to collect from corporate

Canada which has not paid its fair share of taxes. At the same time it withdraws its support of the unemployment insurance program and forcing the small business community in Canada and workers of Canada to pay a larger and larger share in order to finance the unemployment insurance program. It has been a terrible burden on our small business community in Canada.
I have talked with small business people in my constituency in the Okanagan-Shuswap. Many of those businesses are finding a pretty tough time during the current economic situation. Those extra costs of having to bear that burden of UI, of having to administer the GST are placing many of those businesses in a very, very untenable situation indeed. I want to focus for a few moments on the federal cutbacks to the health care program. The transfer payments to the provinces and the territories through this legislation, the transfer payments which have been frozen over the last few years, are going to be extended for another three years up to 1995 through this Bill C-20.
These preliminary calculations show that this total freeze of some five years on these transfer payments for the established programs is going to result in the loss of some $13 billion to the provinces. Somebody is going to have to pay it or else there is going to be a significant erosion of those programs. It places more of a burden on the provinces and ultimately on the taxpayers in those provinces to fund programs that historically and legitimately should be paid for by this federal government. This breaks down over the five years to a loss of some $9.5 billion for health care services. I would submit that there is no way that the provinces can make up that loss without a significant erosion in the standard of health care.
In British Columbia alone that will amount to a loss of some $1.14 billion to health care in British Columbia. This is a significant loss in funding for a province whose health care systems are already taxed to their fullest, and I would submit right across this country.
Government Orders
This is the consequence of this legislation: the erosion of health care, the erosion of post-secondary education, the erosion of institutions in Canada that have become very much a part of the fabric of this Canadian nationhood. This bill is the signal of the end for those programs. It is a bad piece of legislation and it is a sad day for Canada.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to make some comments on Bill C-20, a bill that has been introduced to implement some of the initiatives of the February 1991 budget.
We have to look at Bill C-20 for what it really is. It is a bill that puts into place the working ability of the government to eliminate federal transfer payments to the provinces. By doing so it will allow the federal government step by step over the years to lose control of our great medicare system for one.
This bill, by the withdrawal of funding in a slow and painful way, undermines the Canada Assistance Plan. It undermines the principle of equalization payments to the different programs. It undermines our medicare system and begins to undermine post-secondary education funding and therefore the system.
This bill, and I think correctly, has been called social policy by stealth because it puts into force a strategy by which the federal government is able to reduce significantly its financial obligations to its own programs, as well as transfers to the provinces, while simultaneously creating a mechanism through which it will be able to maintain influence over provincial medicare programs by means not provided under the Canada Health Act.
The government is saying one thing out of one side of its mouth and doing something else out of the other. It says it supports them and then at the next breath it starts to withdraw from the funding and does it in a very devious manner.
Canada Health Act entitlements, through Established Programs Financing, may be withheld by the federal government as a means of deterring a province from violating the act's requirements for national standards. Therefore the established program funding transfers are gradually reduced and the federal government loses its leverage for enforcing the medicare principles. This is

December 4, 1991
Government Orders
what the Minister of Finance was talking about in the 1991 budget when it was tabled and the freeze on the EPF transfers was extended through to 1994 and 1995.
The Minister of Finance said: "I recognize that limiting the growth of transfers under the Established Programs Financing raises concerns about the ability of the federal government to continue enforcing national medicare principles under the Canada Health Act". I beg to ask this House and Canadians: If that is a sincere concern, why did he go ahead and do it anyway?
What has been done? In short, Bill C-20 will allow the federal government to deduct Canada Health Act penalties from cash payments owing to the provinces under any federal transfer program. This legislation goes way beyond withholding EPF entitlements. Provisions within Bill C-20 have the potential to undermine the full range of federal transfer payments. The government can now turn an individual or a business or a city against a province which has violated the Canada Health Act.
The federal government will be enforcing its policies by punishing innocent people for violations of others. I repeat: social policy by stealth.
What are some of the areas that can be affected? Under Bill C-20 the health care practices of a province will now have a direct impact on any group relying on funding for cost shared programs. The list is long. I will just give you, Mr. Speaker, some of the letters that have already come from my constituents and organizations. This is already coming down through the provinces.
I have a letter from Cathy Mates of the Quinte Literary Council which reads: "I recently received a letter from the Fellow Family Literacy Workers and was greatly disturbed to discover the education, community and social services ministry are considering discontinuing social assistance recipients funding for our programs". She goes on to say that it is because the funding is being cut back by the province.
I have another letter from the executive director of the Quinte Regional Credit Counselling Service, Mr. Richard Bower: "Ontario Ministry of Community and Social Services has chosen to cut completely credit counselling services. I was visited in my office last week by the executive director of the Canadian Mental Health Association, Hastings and Prince Edward branch. The enclosed material will give you a brief outline on how we
feel the federal government might play a part in minimizing some of the suffering your constituents are experiencing due to cutbacks in funding". Those discussions went on to say what was happening and that the funding was being withheld from the federal government to the province.
One program can be played off against the other. If a province does not live up to the standards that the federal government sets but does not wish to fund, it can withhold crop insurance funding to farmers. It can withhold funding to programs that deal with disabled persons. It can withhold funds that would find their way into legal aid and compensation programs for victims of crime. The list goes on.
Another impact of this bill is the impact on post-secondary education funding. This very same bill repeals a number of sections and implements a low growth strategy in transfer payments to the provinces.
We all know it is quite conceivable that very soon the tuition fees at universities will probably hit $3,000 a year. The government is forcing higher education out of reach of the average Canadian. It is the average Canadian that we need to educate in this country if this country is to have any hope at all of being competitive on the world market in the next century.
Bill C-20 also announces a 30 per cent premium increase in UI premiums. The government said with the implementation of Bill C-21, the UI bill two years ago, it was withdrawing from the financial obligations to the unemployment insurance fund and that it was implementing a plan which would make the fund self-financing. It assured us that the government would make up any unforeseen shortfalls in especially hard times. That assurance has now been translated into two raises in UI premiums.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It was false.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Certainly it was false. It did not follow through on its assurances to Canadians and to employers or employees at all. Since that we have had two raises: one at 24 per cent and one at 7 per cent. That is what the employee pays and, as we know, the employer pays 1.4 times that.
In closing I would like to offer some solutions for the government to consider.
December 4, 1991

The federal government should first continue to play a significant financial role in both health care and postsecondary education. When I say a substantial role, I do not mean to say just talk about it and give it lip service but to follow up; in other words, put its money where its mouth is.
Second, any changes in the financing of health care and higher and higher education should result from federal-provincial negotiations rather than being imposed by Ottawa.
Third, any new arrangement negotiated for financing health care and higher education should focus on federal cash payments and who has the cash to pay for these programs once they are agreed upon.
Fourth, federal funding for health care should be distinct from funding for post-secondary education.
Federal legislation should stipulate that the cash received by a province for health and higher education is spent as intended.
Just in closing, Bill C-20 is a strategy which focuses on the negative aspects of addressing deficit reduction. It is a negative approach to solving a problem. I might suggest that Canadians have enough negative things to think about at the present time.
It is time for us to use the legislation to generate some creative solutions to our problems. Let us look at creating something good and useful in terms of our program development, tax reform and deficit reduction efforts rather than simply shifting burdens over to someone else.

programs which, after all, were set up in large measure by federal government urging and federal government legislation.
The national medicare system, as every member in this House knows, was introduced by a previous federal government and the provinces went along with it. The second is the unemployment insurance provisions. I want to quote from the former Minister of Finance, the hon. member for Etobicoke Centre, who made in his 1989 budget speech a statement that has turned out to be completely false.
He said: "The government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program"-the unemployment insurance program-"in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build up in the unemployment insurance account". These are difficult economic times.
The Minister of Finance, after months of prodding, finally admitted that we were into a recession last year. It is obvious to every Canadian except the minister that it is not over yet. These are difficult times. Canadian businesses are going bankrupt at record rates. Canadians are going out of the country to shop in record numbers.
I was just reading in the Kingston paper today how there were substantial line-ups at the border. They were people trying to get out of Canada to buy goods in the United States. Maybe it was the Ottawa paper. It was a Cornwall border crossing.
This kind of problem is a serious one for Canadian retailers. Canadian businesses are suffering because of this government's botched economic policies. Yet the government says that apparently these are not difficult times. It has raised unemployment insurance premiums twice, as my hon. colleague indicated, once was in July by 25 per cent which was a staggering increase, and now on January 1 they are to go up by another 7 per cent.
This is economic mismanagement on an impressive scale. To suggest that these are not difficult times and that the unemployment insurance fund ought to be bolstered by contributions from the Consolidated Revenue Fund of this country is preposterous. Yet that is exactly what the government has proposed by this bill.
My friend from Edmonton Strathcona wanted to hear about the deficit. Part of the reason we are in this financial mess is because of this government's inability to control its expenditures.
The hon. member was not running in the election of 1984, and neither was I, but I was campaigning and I suspect he may have been too. The hon. member for Fraser Valley East says he was. He must remember the promises his leader made throughout the election campaign, that when the Conservative Party took office it was going to look after the deficit right away. The top priority was to get the deficit to zero.

Mr. Speaker, I am really pleased to see that we are getting into the Christmas spirit here. It is not even December 25 but we are really getting into "the night before Christmas".
I am surprised because every time we get into a debate like this I wish we could stop pointing fingers and laying blame. The situation right now is that we are stuck with a very serious problem. Hold on now. There are two sides to this coin. I think both sides are right and both sides are wrong, in a certain sense. I will tell you how they are.
It is true that the Conservative government inherited a terrible deficit. It is true that a great deal of the problems we have today are due to free spending by the federal Liberal government at the time. Money was just being thrown out the window. I believed that and I was not running in any election. I was just an observer. I was a Canadian taxpayer and I was upset. I was even more upset to see that orgy of patronage. I do not know if you remember the dying days of that Liberal government, but it was an orgy of patronage where everybody in the know was getting a job and the money was just going out the window.
Since that time we have had a Conservative government and I think that the Conservative government has made an honest attempt to cut costs in some areas. But in cutting costs it has attempted to push the problem over to the provinces and on to the backs of the people who are least able to accept these cuts.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Where should we cut?

December 4, 1991
Government Orders

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The next question would be: How could we have done it? I am quite surprised that the Conservative government would ask someone in opposition because it should know what to do. Unfortunately they do not know. There are a lot of things that can be done. The NDP has had a policy dealing with what cuts could be made without actually hurting the people who are least able to accept these cuts.
We have said in the past that there is a minimum corporate tax that could be levied. We said that over and over. When I look at the United States and I look at the minimum tax that it has levied, I do not see that has had a specific negative effect upon business. Look at the corporate tax loopholes and the reports from Statistics Canada saying it is not necessarily these programs that are causing this deficit. Statistics Canada, not too long ago, said the problem we have with the deficit today is because of the huge deficit left by the Liberals to the Conservatives when the government changed.
That is a result of the fact that the government has had a huge carrying cost on that debt and has been unable to cut government expenses.
If this government really wants to know how to cut expenses, 24 hours ago a brilliant document was released showing ways to cut expenses. It is called the Auditor General's report.
It talks about billions of dollars being unaccounted for and millions of dollars that could be saved. Yet when we as parliamentarians come before this House and say "look, government, we are not in favour of cutting grants to the provinces for education and for health", this government gets into partisanship to the extent that it says: "Well, where do you want us to cut?" It is as if the Auditor General did not even exist, as if there was no independent, non-partisan basis from which it could seek a kind of Rand-McNally map on sound fiscal management. We have that. We have the Auditor General.
I would mention to the government side that some people have proposed fiscal reform even in the Liberal Party. There is a parliamentarian by the name of the member for Broadview-Greenwood. He wrote a very interesting report on a single tax. There are some parts in his report which show that we could have fiscal
reform, generally balance our books, and at the same time not attack those people in our society who are the least able to afford these tax increases.
That is where we are today. We are at a philosophical crossroads. Do we continue to tax people who are least able to afford these tax increases while Canada is being run into the ground? Whether you are Liberal, Conservative or NDP you must admit that when you go to your constituencies people are telling you: "Stay out of our lives, federal government. We are tired. Every time you are active in Parliament our wallets get thinner".
This is what is happening with people from across our country. We are all hurting. When I say we are at a crossroads I am saying that people do not want to see education and health care cut as Bill C-20 proposes.
That is wrong. There are other alternatives. We have given you some. The Auditor General has given you some. I just hope that when you hear these proposals coming from the NDP, the Liberals and the independent Auditor General, you will wake up. The closer you get to the next general election the better chance that you will wake up. I hope you will not wait that long because generally what happens before an election is that the government in power starts to give out goodies across the country to win votes. I hope it is a thing of the past because it is no way to build a Canada.
We do not have what is called "cheque book federalism". I hope the only reason we will vote for a political party and the only reason we will stay federalists or Canadians is not because you have given our particular province more money than another one or because you have bought us off. Canadians cannot be bought but they can be angered. There is an angry mood in the country right now.
The mood is so angry that people in different provinces are getting together and forming tax advocacy groups for their own protection. It has happened in my own province of Quebec and I think they are doing the right thing. We are on the verge of a tax revolution. People are saying: "We are paying more and more taxes and getting less and less services". Bill C-20, which seeks to cut the transfers to the provinces particularly in the area of health and post-secondary education, is an example of the government cutting in the wrong place.

Let me tell you about the feelings of the average middle-class Canadian today, seeing what we as parliamentarians have done as far as taxation and the failure to cut expenses.
In the field of secondary education, in Quebec we have a taux de decrochage or a dropout rate of approximately 38 per cent. Thirty-eight per cent of students drop out of school. The students are our future. They are our future in Canada and right now we are pushing off to the side 38 per cent. That is a terrible number. It is terrible. There is no way that should be allowed in any country. Rather than adding to the financing of post-secondary education we are taking away.
Look at health care. From the province of Quebec's angle, when we look at health care we desperately do want to keep respecting national standards. However, how in the name of Jehovah can you ask us to respect national standards in Quebec when you keep paying us less, when you keep saying: "We want you to run a marathon, but we are going to give you Reeboks made of lead"? You just cannot do it. You cannot carry out the services. The average middle-class taxpayer who wants these services, wants national standards, and wants fair taxation is angry. We are on the verge of a revolution. We are on the verge of this anger being channelled into some very serious demands for reform.
In conclusion, I and my party are against this bill. The reason we are against this bill is because the government has not woken up. It is not cutting in the right place. Unfortunately we will not be able to do much about it except talk until the next election so I wish the government would call an election as soon as possible.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am very pleased to speak to Bill C-20 this evening. This particular bill is one that tries to turn down the tap of government spending. It does not turn off government spending but it attempts to turn it down a little bit. There are a lot of Canadians out there who are starting to become concerned about what the aftermath will be when the government moneys slow down a little bit, particularly in the context of a recession. Keynesian economics shows us very clearly that this is the exact wrong time to cut down on government spending.
Government Orders
In any event, how did we get here? How did we get into this situation where we have to radically alter the way we fund transfer payments to the provinces, the way we fund government programs? Are all of the services provided by the federal government, by the provincial governments, by the municipalities that are funded by these EPF transfers and the other funding mechanisms referred to in this bill continued? The needs are there in education, health, unemployment insurance and others. In the recession these service needs are actually growing. They are not slowing down. Even in the recession they are growing.
Why are we in this position now? There are several reasons and I know we will debate them in this House for many years to come. It is my view that following the 1982-1983 recession, when there was a sequence of large deficits totalling about $167 billion, there was a period of good years, roughly from 1984 to 1990. We cannot necessarily fault a government for a recession. These things happen cyclically over history. We have recorded them and watched them all through this century. However they do occur. They may be a necessary evil. However in this particular case, in this recession we are in now, there was real evidence that the government permitted or induced the recession with its monetary policy through the Bank of Canada.
That was a government policy decision. It is not going to walk away from it. To keep interest rates high was a decision of this government. The result has perhaps been a double-dip recession, not just a single scoop.
In any event, it is my view that between the two recessions, the one in 1982-1983 and the one we are going through now, the government failed to properly address the deficit position the government was in then and it failed to properly manage the economy. It was mismanagement to fail to take account of the growth in the EPF funding structures, to fail to take account of the potentials for government surplus. In the good years it actually mismanaged our economy.
The result is that we have to deal with this recession not from a position of strength but from a position of weakness. Canadians are disappointed in that. They are disappointed in the last five or six years. That is how we got here.

December 4, 1991
Government Orders
What are the result and the impact on Canadians? I want to mention two things. First, and there are numerous ways to look at this piece of legislation, is the erosion of the government's commitment to the unemployment insurance fund. Other colleagues of mine from the New Democratic Party and possibly even from the government side have mentioned that it was clear at the time of the 1989 budget that it was the government's intention to buttress the unemployment insurance fund so that premiums did not have to be unduly raised.
I know it has been mentioned before. However, I just want to mention again the words of the member for Etobicoke Centre himself who stated that the government will continue to contribute to the financing of the program in difficult economic times when it is inappropriate to raise premiums and prudent to allow deficits to build in the UI account. That was confirmed in other debate in this House and in the the other place.
This particular bill authorizes, and we do not want to support that authority, an increase of 24.4 per cent in the UI fund. Having put that in place, if this bill passes we have a follow-up increase of another substantial increase.
Things are now so bad in the fiscal management of this country that the government has had to renege on that promise and on others. Yes, we are disappointed and we are angry. Fiscal mismanagement during the good years has made this breach of promises and lack of preparation for the bad times come to pass now. We have to deal with this as a country.
Second, all of the money that moves from our government to other governments goes to services. A lot of it is delivered through provincial programs. We see it going to post-secondary education. We see it in the hands of welfare recipients. We are talking about the real needy, the real hungry, and the real poor. That is where this money that we are talking about today was supposed to go and now will not.
The government's response is to change the funding mechanisms as if the process is simply a piece of machinery. This government is not bold enough to go to the needy and the poor and say the cupboard is bare.
It is just going to change the mechanisms. It is in fact subcontracting that job to the provinces, the municipalities, the social workers, or the teachers. It is subcontracting the dirty work caused by the fiscal mismanagement of the last half dozen years.
That is what we are disappointed at. That is what makes us angry. That is what embarrasses us a little around here.
To the extent that this government is subcontracting the dirty work, it is doing the job blind because it does not stop to measure the impact on the real poor, the real needy and the hungry. It does not have the opportunity to see what is happening because it will not do the job itself. It does it indirectly by fine tuning, by changing the funding mechanisms.
It is very difficult to be constructive in addressing legislation like this when all you have to work with, all you see on the table, is a knife that cuts. It is very difficult to be constructive and so I cannot be. I can be critical though. I can be critical of how we got here and I can be critical of the impact on Canadians who need this type of support from government. It is a legacy of the 1982-83 recession. It is a legacy of the mismanagement of the good years, but it is still mismanagement. I wish we could repeat history and do it all over again, but we cannot.
We oppose this bill.

subtopic: BUDGET IMPLEMENTATION ACT, 1991 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I too am pleased to participate in third reading this evening of Bill C-20, an act which will cut back on the government's commitment to education and health, as well as other areas.
During second reading of this legislation, I had the opportunity to also speak on this bill. At that time I spoke about the damage this legislation would do to our health care system, our education system, and how it was affecting the ability of the provinces to manage their budgets.
I also talked about the policies the government is inflicting on small businesses. We can see what is happening there. We have bankruptcy rates such as we have never had before in this country.
Today I want to talk about some of those things, but I also want to discuss in detail the government's claim that it must cut back on education to reduce the deficit and make this country competitive.
This government, as we know, has doubled the debt in only six years. It is planning to cut back on spending on

education and health care. According to the government it must do this to reduce the deficit and to make Canada more competitive.
I think it is wrong on both counts. First, the government's recent paper on prosperity indicates that the educational attainment of the work force as a whole is way below the levels that will be required in the future. In fact, it has been indicated and forecast that between 1989 and the year 2000, which is only nine years away, 62.9 per cent of all jobs will require at least grade 12 and 40 per cent are going to require 16 years of training. That is what is going to be required in the future.
Presently we have a work force that as a whole is below the levels that will be required. A couple of statistics regarding the present situation show that 40 per cent of adults have problems with everyday math and reading demands. In our high schools, three out of ten drop out of high school before graduating.
The future competitiveness of the economy depends directly on the skills, training and abilities of our domestic work force. It stands to reason that if a company cannot find the skills it requires to be competitive on a world scale, if the training we are providing to young people is not of a high enough standard to supply our economy with a competitive work force, then how does this government expect Canada to compete in an increasingly competitive international economy?
Certainly there are education cutbacks proposed in this bill. As you know, we have also had cutbacks in research. In fact, the federal contribution to university research and development dropped from 36 per cent in 1984 of the total university research money to 32 per cent.
You would think, in view of all that, that this government would be wanting to improve education. Certainly by its actions and by legislation that it is bringing in, it is doing the exact opposite.
As I said earlier, cutting back on education may contribute to the short-term deficit reduction goals. In the long term it will cost us our ability to compete internationally. It will cost us our opportunity to be truly prosperous in the future. It will cost us jobs, technology
Government Orders
and tax revenue, and it certainly will become a hindrance to any comprehensive, long-term deficit reduction plan.
My riding is in Prince Edward Island. I can tell you that there, where we have a total budget for the province of not much over $700 million, these reductions and funding commitments have a major impact. They have a major impact on a province the size of Prince Edward Island.
Since 1988 my province has lost $100 million due to caps by this government that it has placed on transfer payments. Forty-five million dollars of that is in equalization payments and $54 million is in the Established Programs Financing. It is the money that we received to go to secondary education.
What the government has actually done is not reduce the over-all burden of the country. It is simply passing on the debt to the provincial governments. As I said earlier, a lower deficit would assist in making Canada a healthier economic country. Reducing the deficit by decreasing our commitment to education can do irreparable damage to our future ability to compete and it will harm, not help, our economy in the long term.
In addition to the problems that are created by the cutbacks in education and health, many of our provinces are experiencing very difficult economic times.
There are a number of issues that I could speak on at length which this legislation that we are discussing here this evening will affect. It will have a negative effect on my province of Prince Edward Island, but I want to sum up by calling on the government to really do three things.
I call on the government to re-examine its misguided economic policies which have caused the problems that this government is inadequately trying to address in this legislation. I call on the government to put forth legislation that will stimulate the economy, not stifle it.
Third, I call on this government to withdraw this legislation and replace it with a new economic plan that would make measures such as we are talking about under Bill C-20 unnecessary.
