speakeroldname: Mr. Steve Butland (Sault Ste. Marie) moved:
speechtext:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should establish a national task force to deal with the growing crisis in the Canadian steel industry and the complaints of steelworkers and steel manufacturers, which include a high dollar, high interest rates, and the free trade agreement.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is a real privilege to proceed with this motion. After three years I finally had a motion drawn and I do appreciate the opportunity to speak to the steel industry in this country. I think everyone agrees, all three parties, as well as the unions, the workers and the steel producers of this country, that the steel industry is in crisis. I suggested a task force for several specific reasons. First of all, I wanted to find out what constitutes a task force. I did not want to be so presumptuous as to suggest a royal commission.
A task force is something that emphasizes public hearings. It has a shorter time period than a royal commission. Less staffing and funding are required, and it is much more flexible and less formal than a public and stately royal commission. It is good for quick responses in trouble shooting situations. May I suggest this fits the bill. We are in a trouble shooting situation and the timeframe to address this problem is indeed very short.
I think the task force would remove some of the sensitivities that we met when the member for Selkirk-Red River suggested that an all-party committee address this issue under the auspices of a subcommittee under
December 4, 1991

industry, science and technology. That met an unfortunate demise. I suggest this would be more sensitive to the differences and would bring together all parties in the necessary timeframe, which is indeed very brief.
The precedents are many and there have been task forces on issues of less import. The precedents have been set and some of them are: the task force on human resource development; the task force on tax benefits for northern and isolated areas in Canada and task forces on electricity. The mandate of task forces has been microscopic and probably macroscopic.
Why is it necessary now? All industries, not only Algoma Steel, are in crisis, and most of the industry is losing money in the tens of millions if not hundreds of millions of dollars. May I suggest that only Ipsco in Saskatchewan seems to be doing reasonably well.
The steel industry is the very cornerstone of any country's manufacturing industry. It could be decimated unless some dramatic changes take place. I believe that all players must participate before those changes will take place.
A task force would raise the profile of the industry and indicate just how serious it is. I am sure other people may point out that there are other studies going on. Industry, science and technology is conducting a very thorough investigation of the steel industry, the results of which I believe will come in late spring.
There is a labour force study, a joint study by labour and government, which is very narrow in its perspective on the steel industry. I am not suggesting that we reinvent the wheel and start the investigations all over again. In fact, some of the steel producers have indicated to me that they have all those things in place. That may very well be, but may I suggest it may take something like this to collate all those things and bring them together in one unified package with government approval so we can proceed.
What is in place now lacks any political component. There are no other bodies that can really deal with this issue as appropriately as a task force.
What are the problems with the industry? I think the free trade agreement has worked against us. To prove that fact, the American industry is now exporting into
Private Members' Business
Canada to the tune of 17 per cent. Import penetration is now 25 per cent. Mr. Telmer from Stelco suggests that the Americans are eating our lunch. I suggest they are not only eating our lunch, but breakfast and supper as well. May I suggest to those who tout the dispute panel mechanism that we have lost those rulings. Algoma was put together with Sysco even though I do not think we were guilty of dumping rails into the United States market. Nevertheless we were cumulatively put in with Sysco, and we know the problems with Sysco.
I think the member from that region has pointed out that we cannot sell rails in the United States even though the demand for rails is back ordered for 18 months.
We are selling a lot of steel offshore at little or no profit. We are precluded from the United States and the domestic demand is down. When we have a megaproject like Hibernia and anticipate getting some domestic orders, the first steel order that comes out goes to Belgium. Whether it is dumping or not, it causes the steel industry in this country a real problem.
I suggest that the member from Burlington has been an advocate of the steel industry and we have a steel caucus. It has not been formalized, therefore we are having difficulty getting anybody to listen to us, especially when we go to Washington. I think if that cannot be formalized and we cannot have a committee, once again we come to a task force.
Another problem is that the Canadian steel producers have an organization but times are so tough that one of the major members has had to drop out. What consolidated voice do they have?
Even though it is one industry, we must compete against one another. We have to do that, but I hope a task force would unify the group. We could speak as one and take a look at the problems as one.
For instance, I have had an opportunity very recently to go to the Middle East and China. I learned over there that one of our main competitors, British Steel for instance, has had an office in the Middle East for 20 years. We occasionally send a sales person over there to test the market. It is not surprising it is very difficult for us to sell over there.

Private Members' Business
In China we have American marketers. They are our representatives in China. Even the Chinese have suggested that we deal with them directly. Do we have to have an American middleman? I think these kinds of things could be studied by a task force.
With the status of the industry, they just cannot afford to put any money into research and development. Unfortunately in the good times it did not spend as much as it should have. I am told if sanctions had come into South Africa, as most of us endorsed, it could have crippled the steel industry. Some of the natural resources that we require are not available from anyone else in the world.
It has been suggested to me that perhaps they have been working on a synthetic product to replace those resources from South Africa. Once again, the industry is not in it together so I do not think that is proceeding any further.
It is difficult for the Canadian industry to compete. I think we all accept that. We are competing with offshore producers that do not pay nearly what we pay our people. We are competing with mini-mills in the United States that are extremely competitive. It is becoming more and more difficult for us to compete. But we cannot give up. Surely there must be answers for the Canadian steel industry.
The steel industry world-wide has restructured. The Canadian industry has restructured. Algoma had 12,000 workers in 1980. Now it has 4,000, 5,000 or 6,000 depending on the time. I think the workers are prepared to sacrifice and get involved in a solution to the problem. They are going to require some assistance and I think the government has to play some kind of role in this situation. With the results we would be able to collate the work of this small group of people. We have to get them involved. Again, one of the members suggested 14 weeks of a subcommittee of the industry, science and technology committee. Fourteen weeks is too long. He suggested travel. There was some resentment by committee members. They did not think this was the appropriate way to handle it, that it was going to be costly and just too time consuming.
I could see a task force bringing forth results in a matter of four or five weeks and bringing forth specific recommendations. Study after study after study that has gone on in the past and some are presently being brought forward, but there has been no consolidation of what has been done. I think a task force could collate the material and make some specific recommendations that we could address. Once again, the shorter the list of recommendations that we would have, the better it would be for the steel industry.
We have to become, if I could digress for a moment, a little more aggressive on the trade scene, in particular with our American neighbours to exempt us from VRAs, voluntary restraints, in exporting our Canadian steel into their market. I have already told you the statistics about import-export difference. By the way, our share of their market has been cut in half in the past three years. When I asked the minister about applying the same attitudes and aggressiveness to the American market, the minister suggested: "Well, it is a double-edged sword". I suggest it is a double-edged sword. I suggested at that time that the sword cuts us both ways.
We simply have to become more aggressive. We need more industry aggressiveness, more government support and government aggressiveness. I will never forget my first visit to Washington with the steel caucus group. Basically the Americans suggested: "Keep out of our market. You have your share. You will get no more". Those words were indeed true because their actions since then have borne that out. American protectionism is alive and well, and our response thus far is a very passive approach to our American neighbours.
Some of our own trade officials at briefings suggested: "I do not understand why the Americans do that to us because we are fair traders". I suggest we are probably more than fair traders, but we are not getting what we should be getting.
Another problem, and very specific to Algoma, is because of the amount of imports that could probably be applied to all of the steel industry in this country, we are convinced that all sorts of tubular products are coming in from all over the world and they are coming through at our border crossings. It is a very complex, difficult situation for an inspector to get on and see these loads and determine from where that tubular product has come. To the credit of ISTC and Revenue Canada-and it is good to see the minister here-Revenue Canada has seen fit to instruct the inspectors, to give them specific, instruction as to how to determine which may and may not be imported pipe or improperly stamped. Having given that credit, the problem is we do not have enough inspectors to do the appropriate inspections. A simple recommendation like that could be addressed. It has not been addressed previously but could be addressed by a
December 4, 1991

task force along with a lot of other aspects of the steel industry.
What we have to put together is an over-all strategy. Algoma cannot operate in isolation. Dofasco cannot operate in isolation. Stelco cannot operate in isolation. The parent-child relationship between Algoma and Dofasco we all thought would be a great relationship and a great marriage. Well, Dofasco eventually said: "We are cutting all of our ties with Algoma". That is an indication, perhaps, of how the industry is unto itself. It would be much better if we got in this together, at least on the task force level.
We cannot fight it alone. We need to have government assistance. We have to react now. We cannot wait for any further studies from anybody. Let us collate those studies.
To end this, I understand that the subcommittee on Private Members' Business had deemed this to be a votable item, but when it hit the whole committee it did not go; it is not votable. I am very anxious to hear members of the government and perhaps the Official Opposition to see what their response to the task force would be. It is not deemed votable, but certainly I would hope that members from both other parties would give at least a vocal, moral support. I know a couple of the members in here, by their actions, are indeed interested and supportive of the steel industry in this country. I think they agree that the crisis is now and the crisis must be addressed now. I think a way of addressing it right now is through a task force.

Mr. Speaker, I think the comment I am about to make I would not have made a week and a half ago, but I am going to stand up and speak against this particular motion.
With the efforts that the member from Sault-Ste-Marie put forward in describing the necessity for a task force and the make-up of the task force and also the commentary about the fact that at one time the standing committee-and he acknowledged my part in working quite hard in trying to create a standing committee-
Private Members' Business
with the 14 or 16 week study has done a true in-depth study of the steel industry.
I am kind of suspect now about the fact that when we got to the point we did in the discussion about the subcommittee that the hon. member decided it was not quite as necessary then as his task force is now. I feel uncomfortable in the fact that maybe if we knew there was some discussion about the fact that a task force should have been formed, we could have talked about it.
Mr. Speaker, I think you know that we had the opportunity of discussing the creation of the subcommittee among the members of the standing committee, and also with the industry. We took a look at the fact that there should be input from the Department of Industry, Science and Technology, that there should be input from organized labour, and that there should be input from the management side.
I am somewhat suspect in that for some reason everybody seemed to want to pull the plug on this. That could be for any one of a number of reasons. Hopefully it was not so that we would create a task force. Hopefully they had other reasons. A task force or a subcommittee of the standing committee probably would have accomplished the same results. There was some concern about whether or not the length of time was too long. As the hon. member obviously knows, the concerns that seemed to be out there-and I say seemed to be out there because we obviously will not have a chance now to have a look at them as part of the standing committee- to my mind probably go a lot further. The reluctance of both industry and departmental officials to carry on has me somewhat suspect.
In talking with the executive director of the Canadian Steel Producers Association, along with an official of the Department of ISTC who is very involved with the steel industry, there seemed to be some concern about a parallel study.
Whether or not the parallel study comes via the standing committee, which has the resources and the abilities to study the industry, or whether it comes from a task force, I would think the results would be the same.

December 4, 1991
Private Members' Business
I wonder if the industry would have the same response to a task force as it does from a subcommittee of the standing committee. For whatever reason it has decided not to do it, I am suspect. I am wondering if, because there is at present the study going on jointly by management, labour and the Department of ISTC into the solution, management and labour have taken control of the study and are driving the study.
I am also just as pessimistic on the other side that I am somewhat concerned about the fact that maybe the department is somewhat reluctant to have somebody take a look at the study just in case they do not come up with the same results.
In any event, because of the fact that neither management nor departmental officials were interested in carrying on this study, I do not think we could go and force our way into doors and get a proper job done. What I would like to signal at this time is that when the report does come out from the industry departmental study, I personally will make quite a close scrutiny of that report and at that time make my recommendations to the standing committee of how that report should be dealt with.
The member for Sault Ste. Marie talks about a number of things regarding the steel industry. He talked about the fact that there is not enough money spent on R and D. There is no doubt that industry does not spend enough money on R and D.
We are all aware of the fact that the Government of Canada provides the most generous tax relief to R and D in the world. For whatever reason, industry has decided not to utilize those benefits. We talk about the history of the steel industry and the member made a comment about the fact that there was not a lot of input into R and D or capital cost. There is no doubt about that.
The relationship between the steel industry and what we found in the study of the auto parts industry is exactly the same. I wonder about the protection created because of the low dollar back in the late 1970s and early 1980s. There was an auto pact to protect the steel industry, whether it be the automotive parts industry or the steel industry itself, and the National Energy Program was in place. There was an artificial cost or the manufacturers were paying an artificial price for their energy, and when
it came time to enter the real world they could not compete.
A lot of these things keep rising to the top. I am just wondering if maybe the concerns that the industry flagged when it came before the standing committee are just superficial. I am wondering if all the industry wants to do is stand up and sling mud at government policy but is not really prepared to sit down and talk about meat and potatoes and how we resolve some of the problems in the steel industry.
The member for Sault Ste. Marie made quite a significant commentary about the fact that Canada cannot compete on the labour side. I have to reflect the cost of labour in my own community. We do have a mini-mill that is doing its best to be competitive not only on the R and D side but is changing its manufacturing process on a regular basis. It has quite an upgrading department to upgrade its employees. It is doing everything it possibly can.
What it is doing is paying a rate. I am flexible on this because I do not know the exact dollar, but in comparison it is paying roughly $18 an hour for its labour. Its competition which is down in the southern United States is paying the equivalent of about $8 an hour, so there is a very significant difference in the cost of labour.
There is $8 and there is $18. Like I say, these are rough numbers. The difference is that the $18 in Manitoba is a fixed rate. That is the average rate in the plant. There is no flexibility. At the end of the day or the end of the week you get your paycheque and off you go.
Their American competition, a mill of equal capability and equal age, at $8 an hour is paying a bonus on production. The people in the American mini-mill who are making $8 an hour at the end of the day are probably making close to $20 an hour in comparable funds. Along with that is the fact that we do have some problems with R and D. We do have some problems with the fact that the capital projects have not gone through the way they possibly should have. We do have a significant problem with labour. They are not working together. We have to change that concept and show that there has to be a balance. There has to be a fundamental change in how
December 4, 1991

labour and management work together for the success of the company and the community.
I do not really know how to resolve this right now. When I started out earlier I was somewhat suspect about the fact that quite a significant effort to work a subcommittee out of the standing committee of industry, science and technology failed, and within a week we were standing in the House debating a task force that is expected to do the same thing. I feel uncomfortable about that.
As I said earlier, when the report from the industry and the department is made public, I as a member of the standing committee on ISTC will make quite an effort to study that report. At the end of the day we will be working hard as a government to do what we can to maintain a viable steel industry here in Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have an opportunity to say a few words on the motion before the House by the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie because it gives us a chance to look at the steel industry in Canada today.
The importance of this industry of course cannot be underestimated for any modern industrial state. Certainly for Canada and for those communities in Canada like Sault Ste. Marie, Burlington, Hamilton, Cape Breton and at least 13 other communities across the country, this is a major industry, a major employer and a major indicator of the importance of the Canadian economy. Certainly this industry is important.
It is an industry in very deep trouble. It is an industry which over the last five years has lost some 9,000 employees. That cannot be easily shunted aside, and of course the difficulties facing it in the years ahead are even greater.
When we had the recession in 1982 we thought the industry went through a very difficult time then. Clearly it did, but a recent presentation to the Liberal deindustrialization task force by a representative of Stelco described the 1982 recession as a cakewalk compared to the 1990-1991 and what probably will be 1992 recession. That is apparent.
Private Members' Business
It is certainly apparent to those of us from the Algoma district and from the city of Sault Ste. Marie. We are hovering on the brink of whether or not we will be able to maintain the integrity of the Algoma Steel Corporation which back in 1982 employed some 10,000 employees. It now has some 6,000 employees and the best case scenario seems to be to hope to maintain some 4,200 employees out of that figure. It was almost two and a half times that amount 10 years ago.
As we look at the industry across the country, we see an industry going through many of the tragic and difficult times that the United States industry did during the 1980s. We are told that in the United States various levels of government programs pumped some $35 billion into that industry during the 1980s. In fact, it lost several hundreds of thousands of jobs. I believe it went from some 480,000 to 180,000 during the course of the decade. We are belatedly going through that. When we went into that recession in the early 1980s we were far advanced from its situation.
Why the crunch now? The crunch now comes from a number of factors, but clearly the extremely high dollar value and the high interest rates over the past several years since the free trade deal was signed have been very important factors. The Canadian Steel Producers Association believes that the high dollar has reduced demand by some 20 per cent. It points out that the high interest rates since 1988, since the free trade deal was passed, have made it extremely difficult for the industry to modernize and put in place new equipment.
It is those things combined with a number of other factors. It seems tragic to me that our Canadian producers have to be so extremely careful of ever getting government support in terms of restructuring. Let us face it. Most steel industries around the world get government support one way or another.
I had an opportunity to visit China Steel in Thiwan earlier this year. The whole industry was owned by the government. I believe there is some private participation now, but most steel industries around the world have received government support. If we in Canada provide any significant support that can be identified, we are immediately subjected to countervail by the United States, yet during the past decade it has received

benefits in the order of $30 billion to $35 billion. We have very great difficulties.
When the free trade debate was on in 1988, during that period every steel industry in Canada lined up. This was a solution: nobody could find a solution to the countervail anti-dumping challenges by the United States industry like the free trade deal. Of course that has not worked out. There has been countervail actions and anti-dumping duties imposed on Sysco and Algoma, on the tube division, on the rail division and so on, by the United States.
I guess one kind of starts to wonder: Was this just some minor oversight by the government in negotiating the free trade deal? It does not seem so. In the free trade deal we agreed that we would put to work a committee to establish a subsidy code of support programs that would not be subject to countervail.
Since 1989, in those three years since, absolutely no progress has been made on that. In fact I am told that the Canadian negotiators did not want even to broach the subject, to get into serious negotiations, because they would rather negotiate it under the multilateral trade negotiations at the GATT.
One just wonders if they are afraid to negotiate a subsidy code so that Algoma, Sysco or any other steel company that might need government restructuring assistance would know whether a particular support program of the government is subject to countervail. No action has been taken there. We hope that something will come out of the GATT negotiations in Geneva, which will be concluded in the next few weeks. That would be helpful because clearly the United States industry has received massive government support. Our industry cannot receive support without inviting countervail and anti-dumping duties.
Those are a number of the problems that face the industry today. I am told that the loss to Canadian producers from January 1990 to July 1991 totalled
527,000	tonnes, two-thirds of it to the United States because of its ability, its lower cost of production in some sectors such as mini-mills and so on, the value of the dollar, as well as a very suicidal kind of pricing.
For example, I am told that the United States mills lost $738 million in the first quarter of 1991 to drive down the prices.
We need to study the problem. I believe it should be done through the standing committee. It is all organized to do it. It has already started.
We need more than that. We need government action. We need government action on macro-economics. We need government action in the case of Algoma. We need assistance in the restructuring of the Program for Older Workers Adjustment. We need a commitment on that. We need a commitment on a national training centre which would assist many of those workers and assist the industry generally.
We need government assistance by way of tax incentives for the proposed employee buy-out because we are entering a new phase where we have to be competitive and we have to be productive. I believe that the employee buy-out approach can maximize that benefit.
There are so many things that need to be done. It is important and useful for parliamentary committees and groups to study these matters and make recommendations to the government. However it is important that the government act on the specific assistance that is needed for companies like Algoma, but also act on those macro-economic levers and trade issues so important to the steel industry.
Mr. Bill Kempling (Parliamentary Secretary to President of the Treasury Board and Minister of State
(Finance)): Mr. Speaker, I was not going to speak on this motion but there is some time left so I will say a few words and try to clear up some of the mysteries that have been thrown on the floor.
First, the basic problem with the steel industry in Canada and around the world is overproduction. There are 100,000 tonnes of steel produced in the world with no place to go. That steel ends up in many cases in North America because North America represents the last two free markets in the world.
I just hope that everybody understands that is one of the basic problems in the industry. Another basic problem aside from that is the fact that the industry cannot sustain a price rise. You cannot make profits. You cannot build new factories, plants, processes and so forth.
I noticed recently that a couple of American mills have raised their prices slightly and we hope that it will stay. If it does, it will bode well for the Canadian steel industry.

Let me move on just briefly to the free trade issue. There was no tariff on carbon steel. That should be well known to everyone. Steel was really not part of the free trade agreement.
What was applauded by the industry was that the steel industry would be able to take advantage of the dispute settling mechanism. There have not been any really serious cases before the dispute settling mechanism board.
The Algoma case that is referred to on steel rails and the Sysco case were before the International Trade Commission because they were dumping actions.
On the Canadian and American sides the dumping laws are still in force. We may at some time down the road meld those laws together so that they are relatively simple and stop this nonsense. We have some regulatory problems on the shipping of steel across the border. It is not something that cannot be solved to the advantage of all concerned. It is just that there are a lot of Customs regulations in place in the United States that we have not been able to find a path through, but we will. We are working on it.
As far as the dispute settling mechanism is concerned, we gave ourselves five years under the FTA to determine the definition of a subsidy. We said that if it was not done in five years we would extend it for another two years. There is a seven-year period to define what we mean by subsidy.
At the same time we have these multilateral discussions going on at GATT. Subsidy is being discussed there as well. I have talked to my colleagues in the U.S. Congress and they seemed to say: "We think in the final analysis that we will probably accept the GATT definition of subsidy and that will sort the matter out as far as we are concerned''. I suspect that down the road that is what is going to happen.
The advantage of the dispute settling mechanism is this. A panel is chosen, five members from each side, five Americans and five Canadians. Then the combined group is given a list of individuals, both Canadian and American. From that list they choose a chairman. To me that is a much better arrangement than going before the International Trade Commission where we appear as a supplicant before the court. Using the dispute settling

mechanism will in time be the best thing we ever did for the steel industry, and many others as well.
Statistics are strange animals. People can twist them to mean anything they want. However, the fact is that whether you look at it on a tonnage or a dollar point of view we are shipping more steel into the United States than it is shipping into Canada. Our largest steel customer is the United States. We are its largest steel customer, but we still have a step up on them because we are exporting more steel into the United States than it is into Canada.
What happened to the balances recently was that there was a steel strike. It came at a time when General Motors was placing its fall orders for steel for its new run of automobiles. The result was that the mill it had been buying from was not able to supply. The other mill it could have bought from had a full order book. Consequently it bought the bulk of that steel in the United States and Germany. That is what happened. That is why the statistics are distorted.

The hon. member does not seem to want to believe that. I think if he really delved into it he would find that is the case.
There is some light at the end of the tunnel for some of our mills in this country. Many mills are a fact of life. They are going to be here for a long while. There are more being established all over the world and the only thing we have to worry about is where they are going to get their feedstock. Most of them use car hulks. Maybe if we wanted to help the steel industry we would find some way to get more car hulks into the industry rather than importing them from the United States as we do.
The problem the steel industry is having right now is the debt to equity ratio. It has gone out of the country where money is cheaper, in Japan and in some cases Germany. It has borrowed sums of money, bought technology and put new mechanisms in place. Dofasco will be opening one down in the Windsor area. It has combined with NKK and National Steel to form a production facility that will produce steel that is coated on one side with zinc. Stelco has just opened its z line. Those plants and that production are designated for the automobile industry. It has spent sizeable sums of money. It has borrowed money offshore. It has a debt to equity ratio that it has to watch very carefully, but I am convinced that it has the machinery, the equipment and the market there to deal with this.

Turning to the market for steel production in Canada, I might say that 85 per cent of it is consumed in Canada. Only 15 per cent of it is exported. We should not get all exercised. We would like to export more steel than we do right now, and I believe we will. Under the free trade agreement there are no quotas. There are no quotas. There is no 3 per cent of the market. We can export steel into the United States and we are doing it every day. We are doing quite well with it.
I know my friend from the Sault is upset about Algoma. I am upset about it as well, as are others. However the fact is that it acquired more debt than it could handle and it has some serious problems. We hope Algoma survives, but I do not know whether there are many people who are really convinced it will. We hope it does.
As far as the government putting money into the industry is concerned, I think that would not be a good move on our part. If you are going to offend your largest market for your product, why do it? I mean perhaps you just want to fight, you want to holler and get up in the House of Commons and make speeches about how bad the Americans are. I know that is the great line of the
NDP, that the Americans are bad. But the fact is that they are our largest customer. If we put money into the steel industry we are going to be looked upon as subsidizing that industry. I do not think we can do that at this particular time.
With those few comments I will conclude. I just might say as far as this task force is concerned that I think the wise thing to do would be to wait for the report from industry, science and technology and then strike a subcommittee on trade and commerce to study that report. Then, having studied that report, you have some knowledge and you can go on to do what you please from there.
